nuance.usage_note: Americans use floodwater mostly in news, weather and disaster contexts, like floodwater rising in the streets. It is a mass noun, so say some floodwater, not a floodwater. In casual talk people often just say the water.

distinctions.note: Flood can mean the event or a great overflow; floodwater is specifically the water itself.
Runoff is rain or snowmelt flowing over the ground toward streams, not necessarily an overflow or a disaster.

examples.everyday: Our basement got soaked with floodwater after the storm last week.
examples.professional: Crews are pumping standing floodwater out of the underpass before inspecting the road.
examples.analytical: The biblical flood narrative describes floodwater covering the earth, a story theologians read as both judgment and new beginning.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathtub that overflows and keeps spreading across the whole floor.
nuance.etymology: From flood (Old English flōd) and water (Old English wæter).
common_mistakes: Saying a floodwater or floodwaters for one event; the mass form is standard.
Writing flood water as two words in formal writing; Americans often write it as one word.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew mabbul (flood, deluge) appears in Genesis 6:17, where God says he will bring a flood of waters upon the earth. Genesis 7:17 says the flood continued forty days upon the earth, with the waters rising until the mountains were covered. Psalm 32:6 says that in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach the godly person who prays.

senses.definition: That can be folded.
Something that can be folded.
senses.example: The store sells a foldable for travelers who need a compact stroller.

senses.definition: A mobile phone that can be folded up when not in use.
senses.example: She bought a foldable that opens into a tablet-sized screen for reading news.

core.definition: Able to be folded flat or compact, so it takes up less space when not in use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FOHL. The ending '-able' is reduced to 'uh-bul,' not 'ay-bul.' The IPA in the list had a secondary stress that is not used here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It usually describes products and is a selling point in marketing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'foldable' for furniture, strollers, phones and screens, as in 'a foldable bike.' For a phone, Americans often say 'foldable phone' or simply 'a foldable.' 'Collapsible' is used for items that fold into a smaller frame, like a tent, so choose according to the object.

distinctions.note: 'Collapsible' describes items that fold or telescope into a smaller shape, often with a frame, while 'foldable' suggests flat folding.
'Portable' means easy to carry, while 'foldable' means it can be made flatter or smaller; an item can be one, the other, or both.

examples.everyday: This stroller is foldable, so it fits in the trunk when we go to the park.
examples.professional: We're testing a foldable screen for the mobile app, so the layout has to work at two different sizes.
examples.analytical: A foldable device is philosophically interesting because it challenges what we count as one object.

nuance.analogy: A foldable item is like a paper map: large when open, small and easy to carry when closed.
nuance.etymology: From 'fold' (Old English 'fealdan') plus the suffix '-able,' meaning capable of being.
common_mistakes: Saying 'foldable' with the stress on -able; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'foldable' for things that collapse into a frame; 'collapsible' is often the better word for tents or chairs.

senses.definition: The tales, legends, superstitions, and traditions of a particular ethnic population.
senses.example: The village elders shared folklore about river spirits that protected local fishermen.

senses.definition: The tales, superstitions etc. of any particular group or community.
senses.example: Her grandmother knew a lot of folklore about wolves and the seasons of the moon.

senses.definition: The collective of proofs or techniques which are widely known among mathematicians, but have never been formally published.
senses.example: Every graduate student learns the folklore of the field, though none of it appears in textbooks.

core.definition: The traditional stories, legends, beliefs, customs, and sayings passed down within a particular community, usually without a written source.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then say 'lore' with an r at the end, which Americans pronounce clearly. The vowel in 'lore' is the same as in 'door' and 'store' for most speakers.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes traditional stories without judging whether they are true, though it can sound slightly dismissive if used of a belief someone holds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use folklore for family stories, local legends, and cultural traditions, as in 'the folklore of the Appalachian region'. Modern urban legends are often called urban folklore. In mathematics, folklore refers to results that experts know and use but that were never formally published. The word is uncountable in most uses.

distinctions.note: Myth often refers to a sacred or foundational story, while folklore is wider and includes everyday legends, sayings, and superstitions.
A legend is a specific story, often about a historical person or place; folklore is the whole body of such traditions.

examples.everyday: My grandmother had a lot of family folklore about the farm, like the story of the flood that never happened.
examples.professional: Our team jokes that the flaky test has become part of the office folklore, because nobody remembers how it started.
examples.analytical: Historians of religion distinguish folklore from doctrine, though the two constantly shape each other.

nuance.analogy: Folklore is like a river of stories: it flows from person to person and changes shape along the way.
nuance.etymology: Coined in 1846 by the English antiquary William John Thoms from folk and lore.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'lore' like 'lower', which is a different word.
Using folklore as a countable noun, as in 'many folklores'; say 'many traditions' or 'many folk tales' instead.

folklore.etymology: From *folk* + *lore*, to replace terms such as "popular antiquities".

senses.definition: To incite or cause troublesome acts; to encourage; to instigate.
senses.example: He was arrested for fomenting a riot; after all, it's bad enough being in a riot but starting one is much worse.

senses.definition: To apply a poultice to; to bathe with a cloth or sponge.
senses.example: The nurse began to foment the swollen ankle with warm cloths soaked in herbal water.

senses.definition: Fomentation.
senses.example: The doctor recommended a warm foment for the sprain, to be applied twice daily.

core.definition: To deliberately stir up or encourage trouble, rebellion, or unrest among people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MENT. The first vowel is a long 'oh,' and do not pronounce the final t as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying deliberate and often harmful stirring up of conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'foment' mainly in news writing, political commentary, and formal essays, not in casual speech. It almost always has a negative sense of inciting trouble. Everyday speakers are more likely to say 'stir up' or 'cause trouble.' The medical sense of applying a warm compress is rare in American English.

distinctions.note: Incite is more direct and often used for immediate action, while foment suggests slowly building up unrest over time.
Stir up is common and informal, while foment is formal and implies a more calculated effort.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves to foment arguments at family dinners, so I just stay quiet.
examples.professional: The vendor was accused of fomenting panic among our customers with misleading emails.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that the pamphlets did more than report events; they deliberately fomented revolt among the colonists.

nuance.analogy: Like blowing on dying embers until they flare into a fire, fomenting slowly builds unrest into open conflict.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'fomentum' (warm poultice), from 'fovere' (to warm).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'foment' with 'ferment,' which means fermentation or growing agitation without deliberate blame.
Using 'foment' for neutral encouragement; it is almost always negative.

foment.etymology: From Middle English *fomenten*, a borrowing from Old French *fomenter*, from Late Latin *fōmentō*, from Latin *fōmentum* (“lotion”), from *foveō* (“heat, cherish”).

senses.definition: To engage in frivolous behavior; to monkey around.
senses.example: Stop fooling around and help me finish the presentation before midnight.

senses.definition: To waste time.
To engage in casual or flirtatious sexual acts.
senses.example: Jake has been fooling around with a married woman.

senses.definition: To engage in adultery; to play around.
senses.example: Rumors spread that he had been fooling around with a coworker.

core.definition: To behave in a silly or playful way, or to waste time instead of doing serious work.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on around, with secondary stress on fool. The reduced around is 'uh-ROWND', not 'ar-ound'; link the words smoothly as 'fool-uh-ROWND'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative when it means goofing off. The sexual or cheating sense is informal and can be sensitive, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say fool around with friends, kids, or on a phone to mean goof off or play. A teacher might tell students to stop fooling around, and someone might reply, 'Sorry, I was just fooling around.' The sense of casual sex or infidelity is informal and can be offensive at work, so avoid it in professional settings. Fool around with can also mean tinker with or play with something, as in 'fool around with the settings.'

distinctions.note: Mess around is similar but emphasizes aimless tinkering or messing with something; fool around more often implies goofing off.
Goof off means to waste time at work or school; it is a more direct everyday term for avoiding work.
Horse around suggests rough, physical playing; fool around is more general.

examples.everyday: Stop fooling around and help me carry these groceries, please.
examples.professional: We spent the morning fooling around with the settings instead of testing the model.
examples.analytical: The novel fools around with chronology, letting the narrator contradict his own timeline without apology.

nuance.analogy: Fooling around is like a dog chasing its tail: lots of motion, but very little going anywhere.
nuance.etymology: Combines the verb particle around with fool, from Old French fol.
common_mistakes: Adding with when you mean goof off; 'fool around' alone is enough, while 'fool around with' means tinker or play with something.
Pronouncing around with a clear 'ar' vowel; it is reduced to 'uh-ROWND'.

senses.definition: The act or process of forestalling; a delay; hindrance; prevention; aversion.
senses.example: The city's forestallment of the strike came through an early, generous pay offer.

core.definition: The act of preventing something or stopping it from happening by acting first in advance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STALL. The first syllable is FOR, with an r you should keep clearly pronounced, and the final -ment is a weak, reduced syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a preventive act and does not judge whether the prevention is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in conversation; they say prevention, or use the verb forestall, which is much more common. You will mostly meet forestallment in formal writing, legal or policy discussions, and literary prose. To sound natural, say we want to forestall the problem rather than we want forestallment of the problem.

distinctions.note: Prevention is the everyday, general word for stopping something from happening; forestallment is more formal and suggests acting ahead of a specific threat.
Delay means making something happen later; forestallment means stopping or heading off something before it begins, though it can also mean a hindrance.

examples.professional: The early patch was a forestallment of further outages during the holiday traffic spike.
examples.analytical: Such a policy is less a cure than a forestallment of the crisis it claims to resolve.

nuance.analogy: Like a goalie moving to block a shot before it is taken, forestallment stops a problem by getting in front of it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English forestallen, from fore- (before) and stall (to place or to block), influenced by the older sense of intercepting goods before they reached market.
common_mistakes: Using forestallment as a common everyday noun instead of prevention.
Stressing the second syllable of forestall incorrectly as FOR-stall-ment with a long vowel.

senses.definition: The quality of being formless.

core.definition: The state of having no definite shape, structure or organization; lacking a recognizable form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FORM, and the r is clearly pronounced. The last two syllables are weak, so the word ends in a soft 'nuhs' rather than 'ness'. Don't insert an extra vowel after 'form' (not 'form-uh-less').

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes an absence of shape or order, which can be neutral in art and philosophy but negative when it suggests disorder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formlessness mostly in writing, philosophy, art criticism and religious discussion rather than in casual talk. In everyday speech they would more often say 'shapeless', 'disorganized' or 'a mess'. Used positively, it can describe an open, fluid style or a spiritual openness beyond concepts.

distinctions.note: Shapelessness usually describes physical things such as a loose garment or a lump of material; formlessness is broader and can describe ideas, styles or whole systems.
Chaos suggests active turbulence and disorder; formlessness only means the absence of a definite structure, which may be calm or still.

collocations: the formlessness of the early universe
the formlessness of the first draft

examples.everyday: After we moved out, the empty apartment had a strange formlessness, with boxes stacked everywhere and nowhere to sit.
examples.professional: The first draft of the project plan had a formlessness that made it hard to tell who owned which task.
examples.analytical: Some mystics describe the divine as a formlessness that exceeds every concept we form of it.

nuance.analogy: Like wet clay before a potter's hands give it a shape, formlessness is material that has not yet taken its intended form.
nuance.etymology: From form, from Latin forma 'shape', plus the suffixes -less and -ness.
common_mistakes: Adding extra syllables after 'form', as in 'form-uh-less-ness'.
Confusing it with 'formality', which refers to proper procedure or conventional manners, not lack of shape.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word tohu, meaning formless, empty or waste, appears in Genesis 1:2, where the RSV describes the earth as 'without form and void' before God brings order to it; it is paired with bohu, another word for emptiness. Jeremiah 4:23 uses tohu in a vision of creation undone, where the earth is seen as formless and void again. Isaiah 45:18 contrasts God's act of creating the earth to be inhabited with the idea of a formless waste.

senses.definition: The capability of an electronic device, a piece of software, etc. to interoperate with anticipated future systems.

core.definition: The ability of a device, software or system to work with future versions or systems that do not exist yet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOR in 'forward' and on BIL in 'compatibility', so the -ward ending is a quick reduced r-sound, not 'wahd'. The t in 'compatibility' is a flap, closer to a soft d, between two vowels.

nuance.connotation: Positive in engineering. It is treated as a design goal that shows foresight, though it can be overpromised if a team cannot test future behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers, architects and product managers use this term in design reviews, specifications and documentation. Outside tech it sounds jargon-heavy, so in ordinary conversation people say the new version will work with the old one. A natural reply in a meeting is 'Good, that protects us from breaking clients later.'

distinctions.note: Backward compatibility means new software still works with older data or versions, while forward compatibility means older software can handle newer data or versions it was not built for.
Interoperability describes systems working together now, whereas forward compatibility specifically anticipates future systems and changes.

examples.everyday: My new phone case is supposed to fit the next couple of models too, so it has some forward compatibility.
examples.professional: We designed the API with forward compatibility in mind, so new optional fields won't break existing clients.
examples.analytical: A protocol that safely ignores unknown fields shows forward compatibility, whereas strict schema validation sacrifices it.

nuance.analogy: Like a power strip that still fits the plug of a device you buy in five years.
nuance.etymology: 'Forward' comes from Old English foreweard, meaning toward the front; 'compatible' comes from medieval Latin compatibilis, able to exist together.
common_mistakes: Using 'forward compatibility' for the opposite idea; forward means future, backward means older.
Stressing 'com-PAT' instead of 'com-pat-i-BIL-i-ty' with the main stress on the BIL syllable.

senses.definition: In a foul manner; revoltingly.
senses.example: The stale sandwich smelled foully, so we threw it away before anyone tasted it.

core.definition: In a very unpleasant, disgusting or wicked way, often through treachery or cruelty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ly is a light 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It suggests cruelty, treachery or disgust, so it sounds dramatic in ordinary speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use foully mainly in news, crime writing, novels and formal storytelling, as in 'foully murdered' or 'foully betrayed.' In everyday conversation, awfully, really gross or nasty is more natural. Using it casually can sound overly dramatic, so save it for serious or literary moments.

distinctions.note: Wickedly emphasizes moral evil or mischief, while foully stresses disgust, treachery or a degraded quality.
Foul is the everyday adjective for unpleasant smells, weather or moods, while foully is an adverb used mainly for serious or dramatic wrongs.

examples.everyday: The dog's bed smelled foully after the rain, so we threw the whole thing out in the trash.
examples.professional: Our analysts found the sensor data foully corrupted, so the whole batch needs to be reprocessed before the report goes out.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator describes the city's streets as foully corrupt, a moral claim about its institutions rather than a plain description of sanitation.

nuance.analogy: Like a stain that refuses to wash out: the adverb suggests something has gone wrong in a way that feels deliberate and hard to undo.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective foul, from Old English fūl meaning rotten or dirty, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using foully for a plain bad smell; it sounds far too dramatic and suggests cruelty or treachery.
Confusing it with fowl-ly or spelling it with a single l; the form is foully.

senses.definition: Having four legs.
An animal that has four legs.
senses.example: The shelter adopts out more four-legged residents than any other rescue group in town.

senses.definition: An intersection where two roads cross.
senses.example: Traffic backs up every evening at the four-legged intersection near the mall.

core.definition: Having four legs, as most mammals and many other animals do.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEG, and the final -ged is a single reduced syllable, so it sounds like LEG-id, not leg-ED. Keep the r in fohr.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to warm. When used of pets, it sounds friendly and a little playful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use four-legged most often for animals, especially pets; 'my four-legged friend' is a common, affectionate way to refer to a dog or cat. It also describes furniture, such as a four-legged table or stool. In formal or scientific writing, people prefer quadruped for animals.

distinctions.note: Quadruped is a technical zoology term for an animal that walks on four legs; four-legged is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's four-legged friend, a golden retriever, greeted everybody at the park.
examples.professional: The robotics team is testing a four-legged robot that can climb the stairs in our warehouse.
examples.analytical: The evolution of the four-legged body plan shaped how early land vertebrates moved, fed and survived.

nuance.analogy: A four-legged table is like a card table: four legs spread the weight evenly so it stays steady, where three might wobble.
nuance.etymology: Four (from Old English feower) plus leg (from Old Norse leggr) plus -ed.
common_mistakes: Saying four-legs or four legged without the hyphen before a noun.
Using quadruped in casual conversation, which sounds overly technical.

senses.definition: Something obtained without any payment, obligation or effort.
senses.example: Nothing in this industry is a free lunch, so expect to work hard for every promotion.

core.definition: Something valuable obtained without paying for it or giving anything in return.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LUNCH, with free slightly weaker. The final ch is one sound, like church, so do not add a vowel after the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means a lucky benefit, but skeptical when it hints at a hidden cost. The proverb 'there's no such thing as a free lunch' is a cynical reminder that someone always pays.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom constantly, especially in the proverb 'there's no such thing as a free lunch,' meaning every benefit has a cost somewhere. Literally it can mean a meal you did not pay for, such as food at a free seminar. A natural reply is 'Nothing's really free, is it?' or a knowing laugh.

distinctions.note: A freebie is a small free item or gift, while a free lunch can describe any benefit, including a real meal, that costs the receiver nothing.
A bargain is something cheap that you still paid for, whereas a free lunch by definition costs you nothing.

collocations: there's no such thing as a free lunch
a free lunch at the conference

examples.everyday: My neighbor offered to fix my fence for nothing, but there's no such thing as a free lunch, so I'm bringing him dinner.
examples.professional: The vendor's discount sounds like a free lunch, but check the support contract before we sign.
examples.analytical: Friedman's maxim that there is no free lunch reminds us that every apparent benefit is paid for by someone, through taxes, opportunity cost or foregone alternatives.

nuance.analogy: A free lunch is like a free trial that quietly bills your card after the first month: someone is still paying.
nuance.etymology: From nineteenth-century American saloons that offered free food to customers who bought drinks; the proverb was popularized by economist Milton Friedman.
common_mistakes: Using free lunch to mean a cheap meal; it means a meal or benefit that costs nothing at all.
Changing the fixed proverb, for example saying 'there is no free lunch' in a casual context, which sounds unnatural to many Americans.

senses.definition: Voluntary choice; (the power of) unforced, uncoerced choice.
senses.example: (insane/worst/best/amazing) use of free will

senses.definition: The ability to choose one's actions and make choices that are not predetermined by predestination, fate, etc.
senses.example: Some people deny that humans have free will, and argue that every thought and action is preordained by God.

core.definition: The ability to make choices that are one's own, not forced or fully determined by outside causes, fate or God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'free', the first word, as in a compound noun. Keep 'will' short with a clear 'ih' vowel. In writing, 'free will' is two words; the adjective 'free-will' is hyphenated before a noun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, linked to dignity and responsibility; it can be contested in philosophy and theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday conversation and in philosophy and theology. 'Of my own free will' means voluntarily. The debate is between free will and determinism or predestination.

distinctions.note: Determinism claims all events are caused by prior conditions, which seems to leave no room for free will.
Freedom is broader and can mean political liberty, while free will concerns the capacity to choose.
Autonomy means self-governance, often in ethics, while free will is about the power of choice itself.

examples.everyday: Nobody pushed me; I signed up of my own free will.
examples.professional: The consent form must show that participants joined of their own free will.
examples.analytical: Augustine defends free will as the source of sin without making God its author.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver at a fork in the road: the road was built by others, but the turn is the driver's.
nuance.etymology: From free + will, from Old English freo and willa.
common_mistakes: Saying 'free of will' or 'by free will'.
Writing 'freewill' as one word.
Treating free will as the same as political freedom.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible shows human choice and responsibility without a single technical term. Deuteronomy 30:19 sets before Israel the choice of life and death. Joshua 24:15 calls people to choose whom they will serve. Philemon 14 speaks of doing good willingly, not by compulsion.

traditions.view: Humans are created with free will (autexousion) that remains after the fall, and salvation is synergy between God's grace and human cooperation.
Free will is real and wounded by sin but not destroyed; grace enables and perfects free choice, and cooperation with grace is necessary.
Lutherans and Reformed hold the will is bound to sin until freed by grace; Arminians, Methodists, Baptists and Pentecostals often stress prevenient grace that restores the ability to respond.

senses.definition: A Quaker; a member of the Society of Friends.
senses.example: The Friend at the meeting house welcomed us with a quiet nod and a handshake.

senses.definition: Brand name of a spring-loaded camming device, now used to refer to any such device, often uncapitalized, as friend.
senses.example: The climber wedged a friend into the crack and clipped the rope to it.

core.definition: A person you know well and like, with whom you share trust and affection, and who is not a family member or romantic partner.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a short e, as in 'bed'. The r is pronounced, and the final d must be clear, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The word signals warmth and loyalty, though Americans also use it loosely for acquaintances.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'friend' broadly, so 'my friend from work' can mean a close companion or just a coworker you like. 'Hey, friend' is casual, but 'look, friend' can sound sarcastic or irritated. The capital-F 'Friend' refers to a member of the Quaker Society of Friends, and in climbing, a 'friend' is a spring-loaded camming device placed in rock cracks.

distinctions.note: An acquaintance is someone you know slightly; a friend is someone you know well and trust.
Buddy and pal are more casual and informal, often used for male friends or a warm greeting.

examples.everyday: My friend from college is visiting this weekend, so we're going to hike and grab dinner.
examples.professional: I'm a friend of the team lead, but I'd still like HR to review the promotion criteria fairly.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility, pleasure and virtue, and argued that only the last is fully mutual and lasting.

nuance.etymology: From Old English frēond, 'friend, lover', from a Germanic root related to 'love'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final d, saying 'fren' as a short word.
Using friend for a casual work acquaintance in formal contexts, where 'colleague' is more precise.
Overusing 'my friend' as a polite address; Americans say 'buddy' or 'man' among men, and 'friend' sounds stiff.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the Greek philos means dear friend or beloved companion, and hetairos is used as a term of address meaning 'companion'. John 15:13-15 presents Jesus calling his disciples friends rather than servants, because he has made known what he heard from the Father. James 2:23 says Abraham was called the friend of God, a title drawn from Isaiah 41:8, where God calls Abraham 'my friend'. Matthew 20:13 uses hetairos when a householder addresses a worker, 'Friend, I am doing you no wrong.'

friend.etymology: English surname, from the noun *friend*, or adaptations of it in other languages such as.

senses.definition: Possessing a fringe.

core.definition: Having a fringe, meaning a border of hanging threads, strips or tassels along an edge, used as decoration.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable with a hard j sound, then a quick d; the ending is /dʒd/, not 'frin-jed' with two syllables. The American r is rhotic, so pronounce it clearly at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes decoration or design and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fringed mostly for clothing, bags, scarves, lampshades and furniture, as in 'a fringed suede jacket'. It is an everyday descriptive adjective, not a formal one. In Judaism the Hebrew tzitzit are described as fringed garments, so the word can carry religious meaning in that context.

distinctions.note: Tasseled describes decoration made of clusters of threads tied at the top, while fringed describes a row of loose hanging threads along an edge.
Bordered means having an edge or trim of any kind, whereas fringed specifically means having hanging strands or fringe.

examples.everyday: I love that fringed leather jacket you bought in Austin.
examples.professional: The brand's new collection uses fringed sleeves and beaded trim, so the photos should show the texture clearly.
examples.analytical: The fringed garments described in Numbers were more than ornament; they served as visible reminders of the commandments.

nuance.analogy: Like a lampshade whose bottom edge is lined with hanging threads that swing when touched.
nuance.etymology: From fringe, from Old French frenge, from Latin fimbria 'fringe, border'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing fringed with two syllables, as 'frin-jed'; it is one syllable, /frɪndʒd/.
Using fringed as a noun for the hanging threads themselves; say 'the fringe' for the noun.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the commanded fringes are called tzitzit (tsitsit), meaning fringe or tassel, which Israelites were to put on the corners of their garments as a reminder of God's commandments. Numbers 15:38-39 gives this command to make fringes on the corners of garments with a blue cord. Matthew 23:5 criticizes Pharisees who lengthened the fringes of their garments to display their piety, where the Greek word kraspedon means edge or fringe.

senses.definition: Foiled, stopped, disappointed. (Can we add an example for this sense?) (clarification of this definition is needed)
senses.example: Her plans were frustrated by a sudden snowstorm that closed the highway.

senses.definition: Suffering from frustration; dissatisfied, agitated, discontent and/or slightly angry because one is unable to perform an action or fulfill a desire, or something happened or someone else did something in a way one did not hope for, expect, or desire.
senses.example: She easily gets frustrated when it comes to financial matters.

core.definition: Annoyed and upset because you cannot achieve something or things are not going the way you hoped.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ed ending is a short 'id' sound, not 'ayted,' and the r at the start should be clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild: expresses irritation and disappointment, usually without rudeness.
nuance.usage_note: Frustrated is very common in everyday American speech, as in 'I'm so frustrated with my internet.' People often use it with with or at: 'frustrated with the process' or 'frustrated at the delay.' Saying you feel frustrated is a normal, polite way to express a feeling.

distinctions.note: Annoyed is lighter and focuses on irritation; frustrated implies you are blocked from achieving something.
Disappointed is about hopes that were not met; frustrated adds the sense of being blocked and irritated by obstacles.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm a bit frustrated because the printer jammed again.
examples.professional: I'm frustrated that the deployment slipped, but I think we can fix it by Thursday.
examples.analytical: Readers who expect certainty from the text are often frustrated by its deliberate ambiguity.

nuance.analogy: Like a car stuck in traffic with the engine running: plenty of drive, no forward movement.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of frustrate, from Latin frustrari.
common_mistakes: Saying 'frustrated of' or 'frustrated for'; use 'frustrated with' or 'frustrated at.'
Confusing frustrated with frustrating: I am frustrated, but the situation is frustrating.

conversation.text: I'm so frustrated with this printer. It never works!
She's frustrated because she's been applying for months with no luck.
Don't get frustrated; learning a language takes time.

senses.definition: To hit someone with a club.
To harshly criticize someone.

core.definition: To criticize someone harshly and publicly, or, in rare older use, to beat someone with a club.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'ih'. The final syllable rhymes with 'late' and ends with a clear 't'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes harsh attacks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word in conversation. It appears in old or literary writing to describe harsh verbal or physical attack. Americans would say 'criticize harshly' or 'tear into' in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Criticize is a common neutral word; fustigate is much stronger and more literary.
Castigate means to punish or scold severely; fustigate has an older sense of beating with a club.

examples.professional: The reviewer fustigated the draft for its weak evidence and loose logic.
examples.analytical: Swift fustigates the pretensions of his age with a savage, unsparing wit.

nuance.analogy: To fustigate someone is like striking them with a heavy stick of words rather than a gentle tap.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'fustigare' (to beat with a stick), from Latin 'fustis' (a cudgel).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'fustian', which is a different word meaning inflated speech or coarse cloth.
Using it in casual speech, where 'criticize' or 'slam' sounds natural.

fustigate.etymology: Latin *fūstīgātus*, perfect passive participle of *fūstīgō* (“to cudgel to death”) (see *-ate*), from *fūstis* (“a cudgel”) + *-igō*.

senses.definition: A member of a criminal or street gang.
A member of a professional criminal organization (in organized crime): a racketeer.
To act like a gangster; to commit street crime or run a racket.
senses.example: They gangstered their way through the town, shaking down shopkeepers for protection money.

senses.definition: Characteristic of a gangster; admirable and audacious.
senses.example: Nobody expected the shy librarian to pull off such a gangster heist, but she did.

senses.definition: On friendly terms; cool.
senses.example: We put an end to our beef. We're all gangster now.

core.definition: A member of an organized criminal group, especially one involved in violent crime, such as drug dealing, extortion, or illegal gambling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an unstressed American r-colored vowel, so say it as a soft 'ur' sound, not 'ayr'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests criminal violence and organized crime, though in movies and slang it can sound glamorous or tough.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gangster' for organized crime figures, especially from the 1920s and 1930s, and for crime films set in that era. For a modern street gang member, people more often say 'gang member'. Hip-hop and slang sometimes use 'gangster' or 'gangsta' to mean tough or cool, so context matters when you hear it.

distinctions.note: A mobster is specifically a member of an organized crime family like the Mafia; a gangster can be any organized criminal, including street gangs.
A thug is a violent person, not necessarily part of an organized group; the word is more about brutality than structure.
Hoodlum is dated and suggests a petty criminal or young troublemaker rather than a serious professional criminal.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves those old black-and-white gangster movies from the 1930s.
examples.professional: Our compliance team found that the vendor was a front for gangsters laundering money through invoices.
examples.analytical: Hollywood gangster films often romanticize violence while exposing the brutal economics of organized crime.

nuance.analogy: A gangster is like a shadow company that runs on fear and loyalty instead of contracts and a balance sheet.
nuance.etymology: From gang plus the agent suffix -ster; the criminal sense developed in American English in the late 1800s.
common_mistakes: Using 'gangster' for any group of teenagers or friends; it implies crime.
Spelling it 'gangsta' in formal writing, which is informal slang.

senses.definition: A receptacle, usually roughly cylindrical and wider at the top than at the bottom, which serves as a place to discard waste materials.
senses.example: She rolled the garbage can to the curb before the truck arrived Tuesday morning.

core.definition: A large container, usually with a lid, used to hold household trash until it is collected or taken away.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of 'garbage', and say the final -age as a short 'ij' sound, not 'ahj'. The r in 'garbage' is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday object with no judgment attached.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'garbage can' widely, especially in the Northeast and Midwest, and 'trash can' is also common, especially in the South and West. The British equivalent is 'dustbin' or 'bin', so avoid those words in American conversation. Indoor containers are usually 'trash cans' or 'wastebaskets'.

distinctions.note: Trash can is equally common in American English and often means the same thing; the choice depends on region and habit.
A dumpster is a large shared container for a building or business, not a household can.
A wastebasket is a small indoor container for paper and small items, not an outdoor bin.

collocations: roll the garbage can to the curb

examples.everyday: Could you roll the garbage can out to the curb tonight? Pickup is early tomorrow.
examples.professional: Please don't leave the garbage can in the hallway; facilities needs clear access to the loading dock.
examples.analytical: The garbage can at the curb quietly represents the hidden infrastructure that keeps ordinary domestic life running.

nuance.analogy: A garbage can is like the household's exit door for everything it no longer needs, waiting at the edge of the home.
common_mistakes: Calling it a 'garbage bin', which is British usage and sounds unfamiliar to Americans.
Mispronouncing 'garbage' as 'gar-bahzh' or 'gar-BAHJ'; the stress is on the first syllable and the ending is 'ij'.

senses.definition: Not having, indicating, or being restricted on the basis of, gender.
senses.example: The women's sleeping quarters are on the left side of the dormitory, the men's are on the right; gender-neutral restrooms are located in the middle.

senses.definition: Used by or intended for people of any gender; not restricted to (only one) gender; available to all genders.
senses.example: The women's sleeping quarters are on the left side of the dormitory, the men's are on the right; gender-neutral restrooms are located in the middle.

senses.definition: Of words, phrasing, etc.: not indicating or referring to (only one) gender.
senses.example: Many modern laws use gender-neutral constructions like "they" in place of the old, supposedly unmarked "he".

senses.definition: In particular, in languages where words are assigned to one grammatical gender or another: lacking such an assignment. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: In English, most nouns are gender-neutral, unlike the nouns in German or French.

core.definition: Not referring to or restricted by gender; suitable for or applicable to people of any gender.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NOO, the first syllable of neutral, which has a long oo sound like the word new without the y. The ending -al is reduced to a weak ul, and the word is not pronounced nyoo-tral. Gender keeps a light secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a practical term that signals inclusion without making a political statement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gender-neutral for job titles, product names, school forms, names and language, such as chair instead of chairman or firefighter instead of fireman. It is widespread in everyday American English, and in conversation people often say neutral alone when the context is clear. For facilities, the usual term may be single-occupancy or all-gender restroom.

distinctions.note: Gender-neutral means the wording or item does not mark gender at all, while gender-inclusive means explicitly welcoming every gender.
Unisex is mainly used for clothing, haircuts or products meant for both sexes, while gender-neutral is used for language and titles.
Neutral alone is broader and can mean impartial, while gender-neutral is specific to gender.

examples.everyday: There are lots of gender-neutral names now, like Taylor or Jordan.
examples.professional: Please use gender-neutral titles like chair in the agenda instead of chairman.
examples.analytical: Gender-neutral wording such as humankind can seem to erase the sexed body, yet its defenders argue that it keeps the category open to everyone.

nuance.analogy: A gender-neutral word is like a plain white shirt: it fits anyone who wears it.
nuance.etymology: Gender from Latin genus 'kind, birth'; neutral from Latin neuter 'neither', from ne 'not' and uter 'either of two'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing neutral as nyoo-tral with a strong y sound, which is less common in American speech.
Using gender-neutral to mean impartial or unbiased, which is the sense of neutral alone.
Confusing gender-neutral with gender-inclusive when you mean the wording is explicit about all genders.

senses.definition: Noble in behavior or actions; principled, not petty; kind, magnanimous.
senses.example: Thank you for your generous words.

senses.definition: Willing to give and share unsparingly; showing a readiness to give more (especially money) than is expected or needed.
senses.example: She's been extremely generous with her winnings.

senses.definition: Large; more than ample; copious.
senses.example: Add a generous helping of mayonnaise.

senses.definition: Invigorating in its nature.
senses.example: a generous wine

core.definition: Willing to give or share freely, often more than expected, especially money, time or help; kind and not petty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, JEN. Many learners add an extra syllable after the n, but the middle vowel is often dropped in fast speech, so it sounds like JEN-russ.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises kindness and open-handedness, and can sound slightly ironic if the giving is excessive or unwanted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use generous constantly in everyday talk to praise a host, a tipper, a boss or a friend who helps. A generous tip is a standard phrase in restaurants and is expected for good service. A natural reply to a compliment is Thanks, it was no trouble.

distinctions.note: Kind describes a general attitude toward others, while generous specifically implies giving money, time, or things.
Lavish suggests excess and sometimes extravagance, while generous is usually positive and does not necessarily imply overspending.
Liberal in the sense of giving means freely generous but is more formal and literary than generous.

examples.everyday: That was a really generous tip, thanks for leaving it for the server.
examples.professional: Her generous feedback helped the team ship the release on time.
examples.analytical: Aristotle describes the generous person as one who gives the right amount, to the right people, for the right reasons.

nuance.analogy: Like an open hand instead of a closed fist.
nuance.etymology: From Latin generosus, meaning of noble birth, from genus (birth, kind).
common_mistakes: Using generous to mean large or abundant for things rather than people, which is a literary sense and sounds odd in casual talk.
Saying generous with the preposition to instead of with, as in generous with my time.

generous.etymology: From Middle French *genereux*, and its source, Latin *generōsus* (“of noble birth”), from *genus* (“race, stock”).

senses.definition: Relating to genetics or genes.
Caused by genes.
Of or relating to origin (genesis).
Based on shared membership in a linguistic family.
senses.example: Chinese has borrowed several words from English, but it does not have a genetic relationship to English.

senses.definition: Based on a shared membership in a religious family.

core.definition: Relating to genes, heredity or DNA; or caused by genes that are inherited or changed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NET. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -ic is a short ik, not eek.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science, though genetic can sound worrying in medical contexts when it refers to disease risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use genetic in science, medicine and everyday talk about family health, such as asking whether a condition is genetic. It is standard in a doctor's office and in discussions of ancestry tests. A natural reply to a question is I think it runs in the family, or I'd ask the doctor.

distinctions.note: Hereditary means passed from parents to children, while genetic is broader and includes any matter involving genes, including mutations that arise during life.
Genetical is a rare, dated variant; genetic is the normal form in both senses.

examples.everyday: My doctor asked whether any heart problems in our family were genetic.
examples.professional: We tested for a genetic variant that predicts how patients respond to the drug.
examples.analytical: A genetic explanation of behavior must distinguish heritability from causation.

nuance.analogy: Like a family recipe written in a code that every cell reads.
nuance.etymology: From Greek genetikos, relating to birth or origin, from genesis.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in juh-NEH-tik instead of juh-NET-ik.
Using genetic to mean any inherited trait, when many traits are shaped by both genes and environment.

senses.definition: To retaliate against; to take revenge on.
senses.example: She put toothpaste in his shoes to get back at him for the frog he left in her refrigerator.

core.definition: To take revenge on someone who hurt or wronged you, often by doing something similar to what they did.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BACK. 'At' is usually reduced to a weak 'uht', not the strong vowel of 'cat', and learners often pronounce it too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies payback and is often seen as petty or unwise, though it can be playful among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in personal conflicts, sibling rivalries, and sports: 'She wants to get back at him for the prank.' It is informal, and people often say it with humor when the revenge is minor. For serious revenge, say 'take revenge' or 'retaliate.' A natural reply is 'Just let it go' or 'Don't stoop to his level.'

distinctions.note: A similar revenge sense; 'get even' stresses making things equal again.
More formal, often used for governments or groups responding to attacks; 'get back at' is personal and informal.
Stronger and more serious; 'get back at' can be playful or minor.

examples.everyday: He's still upset and wants to get back at his brother for hiding his phone.
examples.professional: The rival team may try to get back at us in the playoffs, so we should stay focused on our own game plan.
examples.analytical: Many tragedies in literature begin when a character decides to get back at someone who humiliated them.

nuance.analogy: Like throwing a stone back at a dog that bit you: quick and satisfying, but it usually makes things worse.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb from 'get', 'back', and 'at', meaning to return a blow against someone.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'at', as in 'get back him'
Confusing it with 'get back to', which means reply or return to a topic later
Using 'get back at' in formal writing where 'retaliate' is better

senses.definition: A disembodied soul; a soul or spirit of a deceased person; a spirit appearing after death.
senses.example: Everyone believed that the ghost of an old lady haunted the crypt.

senses.definition: Any faint shadowy semblance; an unsubstantial image.
senses.example: not a ghost of a chance

senses.definition: A false image, such as in a photographic print or negative, on a television screen, radar display, or telescope, caused by poor or double reception or reflection (from a lens or screen).
senses.example: The rooftop antenna still produced a ghost on every channel during storms.

senses.definition: A faint image that remains after an attempt to remove graffiti.
senses.example: Even after repainting, a faint ghost of the tag showed through the wall.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of ghostwriter.
senses.example: I’ve written both as a ghost for experts and under my name.

senses.definition: A nonexistent person invented to obtain some (typically fraudulent) benefit.
senses.example: The audit uncovered a ghost employee who collected salary every single month.

senses.definition: A dead person whose identity is stolen by another (see ghosting). (Can we verify this sense?)
senses.example: The fraudster built his new identity around a ghost, a child who died in 1982.

senses.definition: An unresponsive user on IRC, resulting from the user's client disconnecting without notifying the server.
senses.example: The channel's most active user became a ghost after his client dropped off the server.

senses.definition: A copy of a file or record.
senses.example: Keep a ghost of the database on the backup server in case of failure.

senses.definition: An understudy. (Can we verify this sense?)
senses.example: She served as the ghost for the lead actress all season long.

senses.definition: A covert (and deniable) agent.
senses.example: The ghost slipped across the border under a false passport and vanished.

senses.definition: An opponent in a racing game that follows a previously recorded route, allowing players to compete against previous best times.
senses.example: I raced against my own ghost on the track to beat my last lap time.

senses.definition: Someone whose identity cannot be established because there are no records of such a person.
senses.example: Officials called him a ghost because no record of him existed anywhere.

senses.definition: A formerly nonexistent character that was at some point mistakenly encoded into a character set standard, which might have since become used opportunistically for some genuine purpose.
senses.example: 彁 is a ghost character from the Japanese JIS X 0208 character set.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of ghost pepper.
A game in which players take turns to add a letter to a possible word, trying not to complete a word.
senses.example: We played ghost on the bus, each of us adding a letter without finishing a word.

senses.definition: White or pale.
senses.example: ghost slug

senses.definition: Transparent or translucent.
senses.example: ghost ant

senses.definition: Abandoned.
senses.example: ghost town

senses.definition: Remnant; remains.
senses.example: ghost apples (a thin layer of ice in the shape of an apple, which forms around it and is left behind when the apple rots and falls out)

senses.definition: Perceived or listed but not real.
senses.example: ghost cellphone vibration

senses.definition: Of a cryptid, supernatural or extraterrestrial nature.
senses.example: ghost rocket

senses.definition: Substitute.
senses.example: ghost writer

senses.definition: An unphysical state in a gauge theory.
senses.example: In the Faddeev-Popov method, a ghost field cancels unphysical gauge modes.

senses.definition: In the form be ghost: not present or involved; absent, gone.
senses.example: By the time the police arrived, the suspects were ghost.

senses.definition: Of a disembodied soul: to appear (somewhere or to someone) in the form of an apparition; to haunt.
senses.example: Legends say the widow still ghosts the hallway every midnight.

senses.definition: To imbue (something) with a ghost-like effect or hue.
senses.example: The dim lamplight ghosted the room in a pale silvery hue.

senses.definition: To continuously cause (someone or something) trouble; specifically, to continuously be in the thoughts of (someone) in a disturbing manner; to perturb, to trouble.
senses.example: That unresolved argument with my brother keeps ghosting my thoughts at night.

senses.definition: To kill (someone).
To gray out (a visual element) to indicate that it is unavailable.
To forcibly disconnect (an IRC user) who is using one's reserved nickname.

To stop communicating with (someone) on social media, through text messages, etc. without explanation, especially as a way of ending a relationship; hence, to end a relationship with (someone) by stopping all communication without explanation.
Synonym of ghostwrite (“to write (a literary work or speech), or produce (an artistic work)), in the place of someone”); also, to carry out (an artistic performance) in the place of someone.

Followed by for: synonym of ghostwrite (“to write a literary work or speech, or produce an artistic work, in the place of someone”); also, to carry out an artistic performance in the place of someone.
Of a sailing vessel: to sail seemingly with very little or no wind.
(dated) To appear suddenly or move like a disembodied soul; specifically; also followed by the dummy subject it: to move easily and quietly without anyone noticing; to slip.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The spirit of a dead person, imagined as appearing to the living in a visible or spooky form.

pronunciation.tip: The gh is silent, and the word starts with a hard g. The vowel is a long oh, and the final st is a clean cluster with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but often spooky when used of spirits. In American slang, 'ghosting' someone, meaning to cut off all contact without explanation, is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ghost' most often for spirits in Halloween talk, ghost stories and horror movies. A common idiom is 'give up the ghost,' which means to die or stop working. In modern slang, 'to ghost someone' means to end all contact suddenly, and it is widely used in dating and friendship talk.

distinctions.note: 'Spirit' is a broader term that can refer to a soul, an attitude or a non-physical being, while 'ghost' usually means a dead person's apparition.
'Phantom' is more formal or literary, and it can refer to an illusion as well as a spectral figure.
'Apparition' is a formal word for a sudden visible appearance of a ghost, and it sounds less casual than 'ghost'.

examples.everyday: Do you believe in ghosts, or is that just Halloween talk for you?
examples.professional: We had a ghost record in the database: an old account that still appears in reports but no longer exists.
examples.analytical: Hamlet's ghost raises the question of whether the dead can return to demand justice from the living.

nuance.analogy: A ghost is like an echo of a person: the sound is there after the source has gone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gāst, meaning spirit or breath, from a Germanic root related to German Geist.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the gh as a sound, as in 'goast' with an extra vowel, or as an f sound.
Using 'ghost' as a verb without a clear object, which may sound odd in standard speech.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the word behind 'spirit' is ruach, meaning breath, wind or spirit, and in Greek it is pneuma, meaning breath or spirit. In older English 'Holy Ghost' named the Holy Spirit, and the RSV uses 'Holy Spirit' throughout. Matthew 28:19 has the baptismal formula naming the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Acts 2:4 describes the believers being filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. Luke 24:37-39 describes the disciples thinking they see a spirit, and Jesus answers that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as he does.

ghost.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *gost*, from Old English *gāst*, *gǣst* (“breath, spirit, soul, ghost”), from **gaist*, from Proto-Germanic **gaistaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **ǵʰéysdos*, from **ǵʰéysd-* (“anger, agitation”).

senses.definition: A gift certificate in the form of a card issued by a retailer as an alternative to a nonmonetary gift, allowing the bearer to purchase goods up to its face value.
senses.example: I bought a gift card for my nephew's birthday since I didn't know his taste.

core.definition: A prepaid card issued by a store that works like cash for buying items up to its stated value.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, the primary stress falls on "gift", and "card" has a weaker secondary stress. The r in "card" is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gift card for a store or restaurant card that can be used like money. At a register, you can say "I have a gift card" or "Can I pay with a gift card?" A gift card is different from a gift certificate, which is usually paper.

distinctions.note: A gift certificate is often a paper voucher for a specific item or amount, while a gift card is usually plastic or electronic and can be used for many purchases.

examples.everyday: I used my gift card at the bookstore, so I didn't pay anything for the new novel.
examples.professional: Please send the gift card codes to the team by Friday so we can thank the vendors.
examples.analytical: Gift cards function as prepaid liabilities for retailers, which is why their accounting treatment differs from that of ordinary sales.

nuance.analogy: Like a prepaid debit card that only works at one store.
common_mistakes: Using "present card" or "gift voucher", which Americans rarely say.
Placing the main stress on "card" instead of "gift".

conversation.text: I got a fifty-dollar gift card to the bookstore for my birthday.
Can I use a gift card and a credit card for the same purchase?
If you don't know what to get him, just get a gift card.

senses.definition: The action or motion of something that glides.
senses.example: The gliding of the sailplane over the ridge looked effortless from the ground.

senses.definition: The hobby, sport, or act of flying a glider.
That moves or changes with a glide.
senses.example: The gliding motion of the skater's arms made the routine look effortless.

senses.definition: Employing flexitime.
senses.example: gliding shifts; gliding hours; gliding time

core.definition: The sport or hobby of flying gliders, which are aircraft without engines.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the vowel in 'glide' as the standard American /aɪ/, not the raised Canadian-style /ɑɪ/ given in the item. The -ing ending is a short, unstressed ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; suggests calm, skilled, outdoor adventure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gliding for the sport, as in going gliding at a club or airport on weekends. For one flight, say a glider ride or a flight. The adjective sense 'employing flexitime' is mainly British; Americans say flextime for flexible work hours.

distinctions.note: Soaring is the more specific skill of staying up on rising air, while gliding is the broader activity of flying an engineless aircraft.
Flying covers all piloting; gliding is a specific form of it that uses no engine.

examples.everyday: We went gliding on Saturday, and it was the quietest afternoon I've had all year.
examples.professional: The aviation club is recruiting new members for its gliding program this fall.
examples.analytical: As a sport, gliding tests judgment about air currents as much as physical control of the aircraft.

nuance.analogy: Gliding is like coasting a bicycle downhill without pedaling, reading the slope rather than adding power.
nuance.etymology: From the verb glide, from Old English glīdan, to slide smoothly, plus the -ing noun suffix.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I do gliding' in conversation; 'I go gliding' is the natural American phrase.
Using the British flexitime sense; Americans say flextime.

senses.definition: To fall asleep.
senses.example: I go to sleep at the same hour every night, no matter when I go to bed.

senses.definition: To be affected by paresthesia; to go numb.
senses.example: My left leg has gone to sleep!

senses.definition: To die.
senses.example: Grandpa was ninety-two, and he went to sleep peacefully in his favorite chair.

core.definition: To fall asleep. It describes the change from awake to asleep, and it is common in everyday speech.

pronunciation.tip: 'Sleep' has a long 'ee' vowel, not the short vowel of 'slip,' even though the IPA shows the short vowel. Stress the word clearly and reduce 'to' to 'tuh' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an ordinary description of sleep, though as a command to children it can sound stern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Go to sleep' to children or as a gentle instruction, but it can sound impatient if repeated. Adults more often say 'I'm going to sleep' or 'I can't fall asleep.' Two other senses exist: a limb that 'goes to sleep' is numb, and 'to die' is a euphemism you should avoid.

distinctions.note: 'Fall asleep' emphasizes the moment of onset and is more neutral, while 'go to sleep' can also be a command.
'Go to bed' describes getting into bed, while 'go to sleep' focuses on the state of sleeping.

collocations: tell the kids to go to sleep

examples.everyday: I'm so tired I could go to sleep right now, but the kids are still up.
examples.professional: I'm going to sleep for a few hours, and then I'll pick up the data cleaning first thing in the morning.
examples.analytical: Researchers still debate why some people cannot easily go to sleep even when they are physically exhausted.

nuance.analogy: Like a computer that shuts down after its last task: the system powers off and waits for the next start.
nuance.etymology: 'Go' comes from Old English 'gān'; 'sleep' comes from Old English 'slǣpan.'
common_mistakes: Omitting 'to,' as in 'I'm going sleep.'
Mispronouncing 'sleep' with a short vowel like 'slip.'

senses.definition: To exceed an unstated limit, especially of acceptable behavior.
senses.example: I don't mind if you make soup too, but asking for the family recipe is going too far.

core.definition: To behave in a way that exceeds what is acceptable, reasonable or appropriate. It describes crossing a limit in words or actions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'far' and keep the r rhotic, so it sounds like 'FAHR' with a clear r. 'Too' gets a lighter stress but should not be reduced to 'tuh' here.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually means someone has crossed a line, though it can be used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in arguments and jokes, such as 'That joke went too far.' It is often a warning or a criticism, so people reply with an apology or by backing off. Common replies include 'Sorry, I didn't mean it' or 'Okay, I'll back off.'

distinctions.note: 'Overstep' is more formal and often means going beyond one's authority, while 'go too far' is everyday and more personal.
'Go overboard' means being excessively enthusiastic and is rarely morally loaded, while 'go too far' suggests a wrong or offense.

collocations: go too far with the joke
didn't mean to go too far

examples.everyday: Okay, that joke went too far, so please apologize to her before the dinner ends.
examples.professional: The vendor's contract clause goes too far in restricting our right to audit their data, so legal needs to review it.
examples.analytical: Mill's harm principle is useful because it shows where state interference goes too far in limiting individual liberty.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who presses the gas past the speed limit: the car keeps going until someone stops it.
nuance.etymology: 'Go' comes from Old English 'gān'; 'far' comes from Old English 'feorr.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'go to far' instead of 'go too far,' confusing 'to' with 'too.'
Using it to mean 'go too much' for quantity, when it usually implies a moral or social limit.

senses.definition: The state of being grainy; granularity.

core.definition: The quality of looking rough, speckled or made of visible grains, especially in a photo, video, surface or texture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The '-y' in 'grainy' becomes a long 'ee', and the '-ness' ending is weak, so say it as 'nus', not 'ness' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative when describing images or sound quality, since it suggests poor clarity. It can be neutral or even positive for texture in food or wood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use graininess for photos, video, film and screens, such as 'the graininess of the security footage'. It can also describe textures in food, wood or stone. Casual speakers might say 'grit' or 'noise', but 'graininess' is the standard descriptive word.

distinctions.note: Granularity is a technical term for the level of detail in data or a system, while graininess describes a visible, rough texture or quality.
Grit suggests small hard particles that feel rough or sandy; graininess describes the visual or textural pattern more generally.

examples.everyday: The party photo looks nice, but the graininess makes it look older than it is.
examples.professional: The new sensor reduces graininess in low light, so the product shots look cleaner on the website.
examples.analytical: The graininess of older film stock becomes part of the image's documentary character, not merely a flaw to be corrected.

nuance.analogy: Like looking through a screen door or a fine mesh, graininess puts a visible pattern between you and the subject.
nuance.etymology: From grainy plus -ness, from grain, from Latin granum 'seed'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'grainness', which is not a word; the correct noun is 'graininess'.
Stressing the last syllable as in 'grain-ee-NESS', which makes it sound foreign.

senses.definition: A small, round, smooth-skinned edible fruit, usually purple, red, or green, that grows in bunches on female vines of most species of genus Vitis and the self-fertile plants of species Vitis vinifera.
senses.example: Grapes give us whole-fruit snacks, grape juice, raisins, wine, and more.

senses.definition: Any woody vine of genus Vitis that bears clusters of grapes; a grapevine.
senses.example: wild grape covering the back slope

senses.definition: Any of various fruits or plants with varying resemblances to those of genus Vitis but belonging to other genera, not necessarily edible.
senses.example: sea grape; tail grape

senses.definition: A dark purplish-red color, the color of many grapes.
senses.example: For those seeking purply tones, the paint colors available include mauve, magenta, and grape.

senses.definition: Clipping of grapeshot.
senses.example: men mowed down by grape

senses.definition: A mangy tumor on a horse's leg.
senses.example: The vet diagnosed a grape on the mare's fetlock and recommended a surgical removal.

senses.definition: A purple-shirted technician responsible for refueling aircraft.
senses.example: The grape on the flight line refueled our fighter jet before the storm hit.

senses.definition: A person's head.
senses.example: Put your helmet on, or you'll crack your grape on that low beam.

senses.definition: Filter-avoidance spelling of rape.
Containing grapes or having a grape flavor.
senses.example: We bought a grape soda and a box of grape jelly for the picnic.

senses.definition: Of a dark purplish red color.
senses.example: She painted the nursery walls a deep grape shade that the kids adored.

senses.definition: To pick grapes.
senses.example: Workers began to grape the vineyard at dawn before the heat arrived.

senses.definition: Of livestock, to develop tubercules as a result of tuberculosis.
senses.example: The dairy herd grapes in its lymph nodes when tuberculosis spreads through the barn.

senses.definition: To develop a texture with small grape-like clusters of a contaminant or foreign substance.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the sample had begun to grape with mold clusters.

senses.definition: (Can we add an example for this sense?) To envy (from sour grapes).
senses.example: Don't grape your neighbor's new car; you'll just make yourself miserable.

senses.definition: Filter-avoidance spelling of rape.

core.definition: A small, round, smooth-skinned fruit, usually purple, red, or green, that grows in bunches on a vine and is eaten fresh or made into juice, jam, or wine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the only syllable, with a long 'ay' diphthong that glides toward 'ee'. Keep the r clearly rhotic and do not add a vowel before the p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, everyday word for a fruit, though it can carry wholesome or agricultural associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say grapes for the fruit in a bunch and use grape as a modifier, as in grape juice or grape jelly. Grapes are sold by the pound at supermarkets and usually bought washed and seedless. The plural is used for the fruit even when you mean many grapes on a bunch.

distinctions.note: A raisin is a dried grape, so it is a different product, not a different kind of grape.
A grapefruit is a large citrus fruit, unrelated to grapes despite the name.

examples.everyday: Could you grab a bunch of grapes at the store? The kids want something sweet for their lunch.
examples.professional: The produce buyer said the table grapes from the Central Valley will be in stock all week.
examples.analytical: In the parable, the grapes ripen slowly, and the image shows how patient care produces fruit over time.

nuance.analogy: Think of a grape as a small sealed pouch of juice that grows in a cluster, like one tiny balloon on a bunch.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'grape' meaning a bunch of grapes, from a word related to 'grappe' meaning cluster or hook.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a grapes' or 'one grapes' instead of 'a grape' or 'one grape' for a single fruit.
Pronouncing the word as 'grape' with a short vowel like 'grap'.
nuance.biblical_note: Grapes and the vine are central to Scripture as images of abundance, judgment and Israel. The Hebrew word 'ʿenavim' (grapes) and the Greek 'ampelos' (vine) and 'staphylē' (grape cluster) appear in the text. Numbers 13:23 describes spies carrying a cluster of grapes from the Valley of Eshcol. Isaiah 5:1-7 presents Israel as a vineyard that yielded wild grapes instead of good ones. John 15:1-5 presents Jesus as the true vine and his followers as branches that must remain in him to bear fruit.

senses.definition: The color of grass and leaves; a primary additive color midway between yellow and blue which is evoked by light between roughly 495–570 nm.

senses.definition: A member of a green party; an environmentalist.
senses.example: Two greens joined the city council after winning a surprising share of the vote.

senses.definition: A putting green, the part of a golf course near the hole.
senses.example: He chipped onto the green, then sank a six-foot putt for par.

senses.definition: The surface upon which bowls is played.
senses.example: The bowls club rolled out fresh turf on the green before the summer tournament.

senses.definition: One of the color balls used in snooker, with a value of 3 points.
senses.example: He potted the green, leaving only the brown and the blue on the table.

senses.definition: A grassy plain; a piece of ground covered with verdant herbage.
senses.example: Children played soccer on the village green while their parents watched from benches.

senses.definition: Fresh leaves or branches of trees or other plants; wreaths.
senses.example: The florist wove pine and holly greens into a wreath for the front door.

senses.definition: Any substance or pigment of a green color.
senses.example: She mixed a little yellow into the blue to get the exact green she wanted.

senses.definition: A green light used as a signal.
senses.example: The conductor waved the train forward once the signal showed green.

senses.definition: Marijuana.
senses.example: Dude, I can't believe you smoked all that green in one night.

senses.definition: Money.
senses.example: He still owes me forty bucks, and he hasn't shown me the green yet.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of green room.
One of the three color charges for quarks.
senses.example: Each quark carries one of three color charges, labeled red, green, or blue.

senses.definition: Of a green hue.
senses.example: He is wearing a green shirt.

senses.definition: Sickly, unwell.
senses.example: Sally looks pretty green—is she going to be sick?

senses.definition: Unripe, said of certain fruits that change color when they ripen.
senses.example: The green bananas will take several days on the counter before they turn yellow.

senses.definition: Inexperienced.
senses.example: John's kind of green, so take it easy on him this first week.

senses.definition: Islamist.
senses.example: The opposition newspaper warned that the green faction was gaining influence within the ruling coalition.

senses.definition: Full of life and vigor; fresh and vigorous; new; recent; young.
senses.example: a green manhood

senses.definition: Naive or unaware of obvious facts.
senses.example: Don't be so green; everyone knows the landlord is cheating us.

senses.definition: Overcome with envy.
senses.example: He was green with envy.

senses.definition: Environmentally friendly.
senses.example: green energy

senses.definition: Of a green party, environmentalism-oriented.
senses.example: The green platform calls for a carbon tax and new protections for public lands.

senses.definition: Of freshly cut wood or lumber that has not been dried: containing moisture and therefore relatively more flexible or springy.
senses.example: That timber is still too green to be used.

senses.definition: High or too high in acidity.
senses.example: This wine tastes too green, sharp and acidic for my liking.

senses.definition: Being or relating to the green currencies of the European Union.
senses.example: the green pound

senses.definition: Subject to or involving a model of open access in which a published article is only available to read for free after an embargo period.
Of or pertaining to a part formed from compacted metal powder which has not yet undergone sintering to improve its strength.
Having a status (as correct, ready, or safe) denoted or coded by the color green.
Describing a pitch which, even if there is no visible grass, still contains a significant amount of moisture.
Having a color charge of green.
(dated) Of bacon or similar smallgoods: unprocessed, raw, unsmoked; not smoked or spiced.
