examples.analytical: Philosophers have long used the shoreline as an image of the uncertain border between knowledge and the unknown.

nuance.analogy: Like a pencil line drawn where the water's edge stops and the land begins.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'shore' and 'line.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'lyne' with a reduced vowel.
Using 'shoreline' for a whole coast, which is larger than a shoreline.

conversation.text: The shoreline here is really rocky, so wear water shoes.
We drove along the shoreline and stopped at every little beach town.
You can see the whole shoreline from the top of that hill.

senses.definition: The quality of being short-lived.

core.definition: The quality of lasting only a short time; the brevity of an existence or effect.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIV, and the final -ness is a weak 'nuhs' sound. The 'lived' part takes a short i, not the long i of the verb 'live.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a quality and can carry sadness or significance depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: This is an uncommon abstract noun found in writing, philosophy, and literature. In everyday American speech people say 'how short-lived it was' or 'how briefly it lasted.' Using the noun in casual conversation may sound stilted.

distinctions.note: Transience is the more common philosophical word for the state of passing away; short-livedness focuses specifically on duration.
Brevity usually refers to shortness in speech, writing, or time in general; short-livedness refers to how long a particular thing exists.

examples.everyday: The short-livedness of that trend surprised everyone, since it was gone within a year.
examples.professional: Our analytics show the short-livedness of user interest, so we should plan campaigns around quick spikes.
examples.analytical: Many moral philosophers have reflected on the short-livedness of pleasure and fame, asking what gives a human life lasting worth.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandcastle: its shape is clear and lovely, but its existence is measured in hours.
nuance.etymology: Built from short-lived with the suffix -ness, which forms nouns of quality from adjectives.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable or giving 'lived' a long i as in the verb 'live.'
Using the noun where 'how briefly it lasted' sounds more natural in everyday speech.

senses.definition: A gun which fires loads typically consisting of small metal balls, called shot, from a cartridge.
senses.example: The farmer's son brought home a Thanksgiving turkey from the wild that he killed with his shotgun.

senses.definition: The front passenger seat in a vehicle, next to the driver; so called because the position of the shotgun-armed guard on a horse-drawn stage-coach, wagon train, or gold transport was next to the driver on a forward-mounted bench seat. Can also be used in situations of claiming other resources such as bedrooms.
senses.example: I call shotgun!

senses.definition: A one-story dwelling with no hallways or corridors, with the rooms arranged in a straight line.
senses.example: Elvis Presley was born in a two-bedroom shotgun in Tupelo, Mississippi.

senses.definition: An offensive formation in which the quarterback receives the snap at a distance behind the center, often with a running back set to one or both sides of him.
senses.example: The quarterback lined up in shotgun, five yards behind the center, scanning the defense.

senses.definition: Relating to shotguns, either in a present or past sense.
senses.example: shotgun cartridges

senses.definition: Relating to the threat of force or dubious means.
senses.example: shotgun wedding

senses.definition: Relating to the use of numerous, diverse or indiscriminate means to achieve a particular result.
senses.example: shotgun marketing

senses.definition: To inhale from a pipe or other smoking device, followed shortly by an exhalation into someone else’s mouth.
senses.example: Dan wanted to shotgun the pipe with me, but I told him no way.

senses.definition: To verbally lay claim to (something)
senses.example: I got a day off because I shotgunned it.

senses.definition: To rapidly drink a beverage from a can by making a hole in the bottom of the can, placing the hole above one's mouth, and opening the top.
senses.example: He punched a hole in the bottom of the can and shotgunned the beer before the game.

senses.definition: To send out many (requests, answers to a question, etc), especially in the hope that one obtains a positive result (i.e. reveals useful information, is correct, etc), in the manner of a shotgun firing many balls of shot such that one may hit a target.
senses.example: Rather than wait for one good answer, she shotgunned résumés to two hundred companies.

senses.definition: To employ the technique of shotgun debugging.
senses.example: When the pipeline broke, I shotgunned fixes across the code until something finally worked.

senses.definition: To hit the ball directly back at the pitcher.
senses.example: The batter shotgunned a line drive straight back at the pitcher's head.

core.definition: The front passenger seat of a car, next to the driver. Saying you call shotgun means you claim that seat before anyone else does.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel in the first syllable is the open AH sound of cot, not the AW sound of caught. Don't pronounce the g in the middle as a separate sound; it is short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is playful and friendly in casual talk about rides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mostly among friends, family and coworkers when getting into a car, as in 'I call shotgun!' Shouting it first is a lighthearted claim, and the usual reply is a shrug or a joking 'Fine, I'll sit in back.' In formal speech, say 'the front passenger seat' instead. The gun sense is common in news and hunting contexts.

distinctions.note: Front seat is the neutral, general term; shotgun is informal slang that is mainly used to claim the seat.
Passenger seat is the precise term you would use in a formal or written context, such as a rental agreement or manual.

examples.everyday: Hop in the back, I already called shotgun on the way over.
examples.professional: Can you sit shotgun on the drive to the client site so we can review the slides?
examples.analytical: The custom of calling shotgun preserves a small social hierarchy in an otherwise casual ritual of shared travel.

nuance.analogy: Like calling the best seat at a movie theater before everyone else sits down.
nuance.etymology: From the stagecoach-era guard who sat beside the driver with a shotgun.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I take shotgun' is understood but 'I call shotgun' is the usual American phrasing.
Confusing the front seat sense with the gun in everyday speech without context.

conversation.text: "Shotgun!" "No fair, you sat up front last time."
Who's riding shotgun? I need someone to navigate.
My brother always calls shotgun before anyone else can.

senses.definition: Given to showers; having frequent rainfall.
senses.example: We planned the picnic for another day because the coastal town was showery all week.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a shower or showers.

core.definition: Describing weather with frequent short periods of rain, or a time when rain falls in showers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'SHOW', and make the final syllable short and light. Americans say the middle sound like a quick 'uh', and the final 'y' sounds like 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes the weather without emotion, though it can suggest a gray, damp day.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'showery' in weather reports and everyday conversation, as in 'a showery afternoon.' It is more common in British English and in weather forecasts, so Americans may prefer 'rainy' or 'scattered showers' in casual speech. It is safe to use when describing weather with short bursts of rain.

distinctions.note: Rainy describes a period with a lot of rain, while showery suggests brief, scattered bursts of rain.
Drizzly means very light, fine rain, while showery means heavier, short rain showers.
Stormy describes weather with wind, thunder or lightning, which showery does not necessarily include.

examples.everyday: It's going to be showery all afternoon, so bring an umbrella if you're going to the park.
examples.professional: The construction crew will delay the roof work because the forecast calls for showery conditions through Thursday.
examples.analytical: The poet describes the showery spring as a season of renewal, when the sudden rain prepares the ground for growth.

nuance.analogy: Showery weather is like a sky that opens and closes its faucet repeatedly, giving short bursts of rain.
nuance.etymology: From 'shower' (rain) with the suffix '-y', meaning having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Using 'showery' when you mean heavy, steady rain; 'rainy' is better for that.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'show-ER-ee'.

senses.definition: Reduced in size as a result of shrinkage; shriveled.
senses.example: A shriveled and shrunken appearance.

core.definition: Made smaller than before, usually by shrinking, or reduced in size or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak, reduced uh, and the ng is one sound with no hard g after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for objects. When describing people, a shrunken figure can sound sad or frail.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use shrunken before a noun, as in 'a shrunken sweater' or 'a shrunken budget.' As a predicate, they usually say 'it shrank' or 'it shrunk' rather than 'it is shrunken.' Shrunken is common in everyday talk about laundry and in business talk about budgets, staff, or markets.

distinctions.note: Shrunk is the usual past participle in predicate use ('my shirt shrunk'); shrunken is mainly used before a noun.
Small describes size in general; shrunken implies the thing used to be bigger and has lost size.

examples.everyday: I washed my wool sweater on hot, and now it's a shrunken mess.
examples.professional: With a shrunken budget, we can only fund two of the three contractors.
examples.analytical: The author's argument about widening inequality rests on the image of a shrunken middle class.

nuance.analogy: Like a photograph that was printed on paper that dried and tightened, the image is still there but everything is smaller.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of shrink, from Old English scrincan.
common_mistakes: Using shrunken after be in everyday speech, where shrunk is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle vowel as a long oo sound; it is a short u, as in 'cup.'

senses.definition: Characterized by a hissing or hushing sound such as the s or sh in sack or shack.
senses.example: The speaker's sibilant consonants whistled through the cheap microphone during the sermon.

senses.definition: A consonant having a hissing or hushing sound such as the s or sh in sack or shack.
senses.example: In phonetics class, we practiced distinguishing the sibilant from the fricative sounds in each word.

core.definition: Making a hissing or hushing sound, like the s, z, sh, or ch sounds in speech.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa. The final t is light, and the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Sibilant is mainly used by linguists, speech therapists, poets, and audio engineers. Americans would describe a hissing sound more simply as 'hissing' or 'whispery' in everyday talk. As a noun, it refers to the consonant itself, like s or sh.

distinctions.note: Fricative is the general phonetic category for sounds made by air forced through a narrow gap; sibilant is a more specific type of fricative with a high hissing sound.

examples.everyday: The kids' whispering was so sibilant that we could hear the s sounds from across the room.
examples.professional: In voice training, I tell speakers to soften sibilant sounds so the microphone doesn't distort them.
examples.analytical: The sibilant consonants in the line create a hushing effect that reinforces the poem's sense of secrecy and danger.

nuance.analogy: A sibilant sound is like the hiss of a cat's warning: sharp, high, and unmistakable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sibilans, present participle of sibilare (to hiss).
common_mistakes: Using 'sibilant' only for the s sound; it also covers sh, z, and ch.
Confusing the adjective with the noun: 'a sibilant' is a consonant, but 'sibilant speech' is an adjective phrase.

sibilant.etymology: From Latin *sībilāns*, present active participle of *sībilō* (“to hiss”).

senses.definition: To make ill.
senses.example: The infection will sicken him until amputation is needed.

senses.definition: To become ill.
senses.example: I will sicken if I don’t get some more exercise.

senses.definition: To fill with disgust or abhorrence.
senses.example: His arrogant behavior sickens me.

senses.definition: To be filled with disgust or abhorrence.
senses.example: Watching the cruel video made me sicken, and I had to close the laptop.

senses.definition: To become disgusting or tedious.
To become weak; to decay; to languish.
senses.example: The houseplants sickened over the winter because nobody watered them while we were away.

senses.definition: To lower the standing of.
senses.example: His reckless lies began to sicken the reputation of the entire team.

core.definition: To make someone ill, or to become ill. Also, to fill someone with strong disgust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, reduced vowel plus n, so it sounds like 'kin' with a very light vowel, not 'ken.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes illness or strong revulsion, so it is used for serious or unpleasant situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sicken mostly in written or formal speech, and in spoken English they usually say 'make sick' or 'get sick.' In everyday talk, 'It sickens me' is a strong way to say you are disgusted by something, such as cruelty or waste, and it can sound heavy if used casually. Sicken is also common in news writing, where it describes outbreaks or contamination.

distinctions.note: Disgust is a feeling; sicken can be a process that causes illness or leads to that feeling.
Nauseate is specifically about making you feel like vomiting; sicken is broader and can mean ill health or moral revulsion.
Make sick is the everyday spoken form; sicken is more formal and more literary.

examples.everyday: That story about the landlord really sickens me, honestly.
examples.professional: The contaminated shipment could sicken hundreds of customers if we do not recall it today.
examples.analytical: Such cruelty, presented as ordinary policy, should sicken any conscience that still recognizes human dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like rust slowly eating into metal, sicken works on a body or a conscience gradually until its health visibly fails.
nuance.etymology: From sick plus the verb-forming suffix -en, from Old English seocnian, to be ill.
common_mistakes: Using sicken for simple tiredness or mild nausea, where 'make sick' or 'feel sick' is more natural in American speech.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'ken' rather than a reduced vowel plus n.

senses.definition: The activity of going out looking at things; tourism.
senses.example: Sightseeing is a frequent reason to visit San Francisco.

core.definition: The activity of visiting interesting places and looking at famous sights while traveling.

pronunciation.tip: Put the primary stress on 'SITE' and a secondary stress on 'see', with the 'ing' reduced. Do not stress the second word equally, which makes the phrase sound stiff.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sightseeing' casually when talking about trips, as in 'We did some sightseeing in Boston'. It is friendly and everyday, and it often appears in travel planning. People may say 'touring' or 'going to see the sights' as close alternatives.

distinctions.note: Tourism is the broad industry of travel, while sightseeing is the specific activity of looking at sights.
A tour is usually a guided trip with a set plan, while sightseeing can be independent.

examples.everyday: We're going sightseeing downtown this afternoon if the weather holds.
examples.professional: The conference offers a sightseeing tour for attendees on the last day.
examples.analytical: Sightseeing reshapes how a traveler reads a city, turning streets into a sequence of landmarks.

nuance.analogy: Sightseeing is like reading the highlights of a book instead of the whole story: you see the famous parts first.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'sight' and 'seeing', from Old English 'gesiht' and 'seon', to see.
common_mistakes: Saying 'do sightseeing' versus 'go sightseeing'; both are used, but 'go sightseeing' is most common.
Pronouncing 'sight' as 'sit', which changes the word completely.

conversation.text: We did a lot of sightseeing in Washington, DC.
Let's go sightseeing in the morning and relax in the afternoon.
I'm tired of sightseeing; can we just sit by the pool?

senses.definition: To create a sign out of something.
To give (something) a meaning or an importance. (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)
senses.example: Her silence signified more than any argument she could have made.

senses.definition: To show one’s intentions with a sign etc. to indicate, announce, or portend.
senses.example: Dark clouds over the ridge signify that a storm is approaching quickly.

senses.definition: To mean; to betoken.
To make a difference; to matter (in negative or interrogative expressions).
senses.example: Honestly, it doesn't signify whether we arrive at nine or ten.

core.definition: To be a sign of something, or to mean or indicate something, often with importance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable rhymes with 'my', so it ends in a clear 'fy' sound, not 'fee'. Keep the middle vowel short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It sounds serious or literary in tone, so it fits writing and careful speech more than casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'signify' mainly in formal, academic, or literary writing, and in religious or philosophical discussion. In everyday speech, Americans prefer 'mean' or 'show', as in 'What does that mean?' rather than 'What does that signify?' 'Signify' can sound stiff or pretentious in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Mean' is the everyday word for what something intends or implies, while 'signify' is more formal and often suggests a sign or symbol that points to something.
'Indicate' is neutral and technical, while 'signify' carries a stronger sense of meaning something important or symbolic.

examples.everyday: When my friend leaves the porch light on, it signifies that she's home and it's okay to visit.
examples.professional: A sudden drop in engagement can signify a problem in the onboarding flow, so we should check it.
examples.analytical: In Scripture, an act may signify a deeper spiritual truth, so readers must consider both the literal event and its meaning.

nuance.analogy: To signify is like a road sign pointing the way: the sign does not travel the road itself, but it tells you where the road leads.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'significare', to make known, from 'signum', sign, and 'facere', to make.
common_mistakes: Using 'signify' in casual speech where 'mean' is more natural, which can sound stiff.
Confusing 'signify' with 'significant' as an adjective, saying 'It signifies' when you mean 'It is significant'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb is sēmainō (σημαίνω), meaning to make known by a sign or to indicate. The RSV often renders it with words like 'show' or 'make known', rather than 'signify'. In John 12:33 the evangelist explains that Jesus spoke to show by what death he would die. In John 18:32 the same kind of wording describes Jesus' prediction of the manner of his death. In Revelation 1:1 God is said to make the revelation known through an angel to his servant John.

signify.etymology: Middle English *signifien*, from Old French *signifier*, from Latin *significare*.

senses.definition: Slender; thin.
senses.example: Movie stars are usually slim, attractive, and young.

senses.definition: Slender in an attractive way.
senses.example: Movie stars are usually slim, attractive, and young.

senses.definition: Designed to make the wearer appear slim.
senses.example: The shapewear was slim and designed to make her appear slimmer under the dress.

senses.definition: Long and narrow.
senses.example: The slim silver letter opener lay on the desk beside her laptop.

senses.definition: Of a reduced size, with the intent of being more efficient.
senses.example: The agency adopted a slim government structure to make its operations more efficient.

senses.definition: Very small, tiny.
senses.example: I'm afraid your chances are quite slim.

senses.definition: Bad, of questionable quality; not strongly built, flimsy.
senses.example: A slimly-shod lad;

senses.definition: Sly, crafty.
senses.example: Don't trust that slim character; he always has a scheme up his sleeve.

senses.definition: A type of cigarette substantially longer and thinner than normal cigarettes.
senses.example: I only smoke slims.

senses.definition: AIDS, or the chronic wasting associated with its later stages.
senses.example: Doctors in the 1980s often called the wasting that came with late AIDS simply slim.

senses.definition: Cocaine.
senses.example: The dealer told the college kids he had good slim for the party.

senses.definition: To lose weight in order to achieve slimness.
senses.example: She started running every morning because she wanted to slim before her reunion.

senses.definition: To make slimmer; to reduce in size.
senses.example: The design team slimmed the phone's case to make it easier to carry.

core.definition: Thin and slender in a trim, attractive way; also small in amount, as in a slim chance.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i as in 'sit', not the long ee of 'seem'. The l is clear before the m, and the lips close firmly at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing people, since slim is usually a compliment; neutral for objects like slim wallets or phones.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often call someone slim as a compliment, but they may prefer slender or thin in medical or neutral contexts. Slim is also used for objects, such as a slim wallet or slim jeans, and in phrases like a slim chance, which means a small one. The phrasal verb slim down is common for losing weight.

distinctions.note: Thin can be neutral or negative, suggesting too little flesh; slim is usually a compliment.
Slender is more formal and literary, often describing graceful forms; slim is more everyday.
Skinny is informal and can sound unkind or worrying when used of a person.

examples.everyday: She has been running every morning and looks really slim now.
examples.professional: We have a slim margin on this release, so any delay will push us past the deadline.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a slim thread of evidence, which is hardly enough to support its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a pencil among markers: narrow and light, with no extra bulk.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Dutch slim, meaning bad or crooked, which came to mean thin in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing slim with slime; they sound similar but have different vowels and meanings.
Calling a person slim in a worried or clinical way; slim sounds positive, so use thin for concern.

slim.etymology: Borrowing from or Dutch *slim* (“bad, sly, clever”), from Middle Dutch *slim* (“bad, crooked”), from **slimb*, from **slimb*, from Proto-Germanic **slimbaz* (“oblique, crooked”).

senses.definition: A narrow cut or opening; a slot.
The vulva.
senses.example: The anatomy textbook labeled the external structures, including the slit, in a detailed diagram.

senses.definition: A woman, usually a sexually loose woman; a prostitute.
senses.example: The old sailor muttered that the bar girl was nothing but a slit, and nobody laughed.

senses.definition: To cut a narrow opening.
senses.example: He slit the bag open and the rice began pouring out.

senses.definition: To split into strips by lengthwise cuts.
senses.example: Slit the zucchini lengthwise into thin strips, then grill them until they turn golden brown.

senses.definition: To cut; to sever; to divide.
senses.example: The wild dog slit the rope with its teeth and ran off into the woods.

senses.definition: Having a cut narrow opening.
senses.example: The cat's slit pupils narrowed in the bright afternoon sun.

core.definition: A long, narrow cut or opening, such as a slot for mail, a gap in a fabric, or a window in a wall.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'i' as in 'sit', not a long 'ee' as in 'sleet'. The final 't' is a crisp, clear stop, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It becomes grim or violent in phrases like 'throat slit'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slit for everyday things such as a slit in a skirt, a mail slit, or a narrow window. Slang senses of slit also exist, but they are vulgar and offensive, so avoid them in conversation. For a polite everyday word for an opening, slot is often more natural.

distinctions.note: A slot is an opening for inserting something, such as a coin slot, while a slit is a long narrow cut made in a material.
A slice is a thin piece cut off from something, while a slit is the narrow opening left by cutting.
A gap is a space between things that may not be made by cutting, while a slit is a narrow cut or opening.

examples.everyday: Can you slit open this package for me? The tape won't come off.
examples.professional: The vendor's fixture has a slit where the sensor cable passes through the housing.
examples.analytical: The narrow slit in the stone wall was designed to let in light without letting in the wind.

nuance.analogy: Like the thin gap a letter slides through under a door.
nuance.etymology: From Old English slitan, meaning 'to split' or 'to tear'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long vowel, like 'sleet' or 'slid'.
Using throat slit or similar violent phrasing in everyday conversation without intending that tone.

slit.etymology: From Middle English *slitten*, from Old English *slītan*, from Proto-Germanic **slītaną* (“to tear apart”), from Proto-Indo-European **leyd-* (“to tear, rend, split apart”).

senses.definition: Food, in contrast to fast food, that is traditionally prepared and normally a part of a complete meal; especially the traditional cuisine of a region.

core.definition: Food that is traditionally prepared, usually as part of a complete meal, especially a region's traditional cooking. It is the opposite of fast food.

pronunciation.tip: Both words get stress, with the secondary stress on 'slow' and the primary stress on 'food'. Make the 'ow' in 'slow' a full diphthong, not a short 'o', and keep 'food' with a long, tense 'oo'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The phrase suggests care, tradition, quality and time spent cooking, and it is often used approvingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slow food mostly when they talk about cooking that takes time, uses local ingredients or follows family recipes, for example 'We're doing slow food this weekend: a braised brisket all day.' It is also the name of the international Slow Food movement, so it can sound a bit political or lifestyle-oriented in some settings. A natural reply to a menu recommendation is simply 'That sounds great, let's get it.'

distinctions.note: Comfort food is defined by emotional familiarity, such as mac and cheese, while slow food is defined by how the food is traditionally made and eaten.
Fast food is quick, standardized and designed for speed, which is exactly the contrast slow food is built on.

examples.everyday: We went to a little place that serves slow food, like pot roast and homemade biscuits.
examples.professional: Our catering client wants a menu built on slow food from local farms, so we're rewriting the recipes this week.
examples.analytical: Slow food treats cooking as a cultural practice rather than merely a way to fill the stomach quickly.

nuance.analogy: Like a pot of beans simmering all afternoon, compared with a microwave burrito ready in two minutes.
nuance.etymology: Coined as a counterpart to fast food; the Italian Slow Food movement began in 1986.
common_mistakes: Saying 'slow foods' with a plural when speaking about the general idea; the phrase is usually uncountable.
Confusing it with 'slowly eaten food' or 'food that cooks slowly'; the phrase refers to traditional, meal-based cooking.

slow-food.etymology: From *fast food*, popularized by the organization Slow Food.

senses.definition: A person who moves slowly or takes a long time to do something.
senses.example: Hey, you slowpokes in the back! Get a move on!

core.definition: A person who moves, works or decides slowly, often in a way that holds others back.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable 'SLOH', with a lighter second syllable. The second part is pronounced 'pohk', with a long 'oh' vowel, not 'pock'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative and often teasing. It can be playful among friends but rude if said to a colleague or stranger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slowpoke mainly in friendly teasing, as in 'Come on, slowpoke, we're going to miss the movie!' Calling an adult a slowpoke at work can sound condescending, so use it only with close friends or family. Among children it is a common playful insult, and a typical reply is 'I'm coming, I'm coming!'

distinctions.note: Slowcoach is a British informal word with the same meaning, so Americans say slowpoke instead.
A laggard is someone or something that falls behind others, a more formal and less playful term than slowpoke.

examples.everyday: Come on, slowpoke, the pizza's getting cold!
examples.professional: Don't be a slowpoke with the sign-offs, because the release window closes Friday.
examples.analytical: To call a cautious adopter a slowpoke ignores the reasons they hesitate.

nuance.analogy: Like the hiker at the back of the group who keeps everyone waiting at every bend in the trail.
common_mistakes: Using slowpoke in a serious workplace complaint, where it sounds mocking; say 'we need to move faster' instead.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'pock' rather than 'pohk'.

senses.definition: To spread (a substance, especially one that colors or is dirty) across a surface by rubbing.
senses.example: The artist smeared paint over the canvas in broad strokes.

senses.definition: To cover (a surface with a layer of some substance) by rubbing.
senses.example: She smeared her lips with lipstick.

senses.definition: To make something dirty.
To make a surface dirty by covering it.
To damage someone's reputation by slandering, misrepresenting, or otherwise making false accusations about them, their statements, or their actions.
senses.example: The opposition party attempted to smear the candidate by spreading incorrect and unverifiable rumors about their personal behavior.

senses.definition: To cause (something) to be messy or not clear by rubbing and spreading it.
senses.example: Don't smear the ink with your hand while it's still wet, or the page will look a mess.

senses.definition: To become messy or not clear by being spread.
senses.example: The paint is still wet — don't touch it or it will smear.

senses.definition: To write or draw (something) by spreading a substance on a surface.
To cause (something) to be a particular color by covering with a substance.
senses.example: She smeared fresh paint across the fence until every board was a bright shade of blue.

senses.definition: To rub (a body part, etc.) across a surface.
To attempt to remove (a substance) from a surface by rubbing.
To climb without using footholds, using the friction from the shoe to stay on the wall.
senses.example: At the crag, she smeared her toes against the smooth granite, trusting only friction to hold her.

senses.definition: A mark made by smearing.
senses.example: This detergent cleans windows without leaving smears.

senses.definition: A presentation of a sauce, purée or other food item, which is placed in a dollop and spread across the plate.
senses.example: The chef's signature dish was a seared scallop resting on a carrot smear and microgreens.

senses.definition: A false or unsupported, malicious statement intended to injure a person's reputation.
senses.example: smear campaign

senses.definition: A Pap smear (screening test for cervical cancer).
senses.example: I'm going to the doctor's this afternoon for a smear.

senses.definition: Any of various forms of distortion that make a signal harder to see or hear.
senses.example: Heavy interference from the nearby substation created a smear that blurred the television picture.

senses.definition: A maneuver in which a shoe is placed onto a holdless rock, and the friction from the shoe keeps it in contact with the rock.
senses.example: Her toughest move on the slab was a smear near the top, where no handhold existed.

senses.definition: A preparation to be examined under a microscope, made by spreading a thin layer of a substance (such as blood, bacterial culture) on a slide.
senses.example: The lab technician prepared a blood smear on a glass slide to look for malaria parasites.

senses.definition: A rough glissando in jazz music.
senses.example: The trumpeter opened the solo with a rough smear up to the high note.

core.definition: To spread a wet or sticky substance across a surface, or to make a surface dirty by rubbing something across it.

pronunciation.tip: The given /smɪə(ɹ)/ is a British-style pronunciation. In General American, the vowel is a single 'ee' sound followed by a clear r, so it rhymes with 'year' and 'near'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a physical action; negative when used for spreading false claims about someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'smear peanut butter on bread' in everyday cooking, and use the noun 'smear campaign' in politics and news. The negative sense of spreading lies about someone is common in news and political talk. For the physical sense, 'spread' is often the more common neutral choice.

distinctions.note: Spread is the everyday neutral word; smear suggests a messier, less even application.
Smudge describes an accidental mark; smear can be deliberate spreading or a damaging attack.

examples.everyday: Smear a little butter on the pan before you add the eggs.
examples.professional: Someone smeared a sticky residue across the lab bench, so we need to clean it before the next run.
examples.analytical: A political smear works not by proving a claim but by making any denial look like an admission.

nuance.analogy: A smear is like a painter's thumb dragged through wet paint: the color spreads where it should not.
nuance.etymology: From Old English smerian, to anoint or rub with fat or ointment.
common_mistakes: Using 'smear' for a positive spreading of spread food; 'spread' is more natural for most everyday food.
Pronouncing it 'smeer-ing' with an extra syllable in the verb; it has one syllable.

smear.etymology: From Middle English *smeren*, *smerien*, from Old English *smerian*, *smyrian*, *smierwan* (“to anoint or rub with grease, oil, etc.”), from **smirwijan*, from Proto-Germanic **smirwijaną*.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, snaps.
senses.example: a snapper-up of bargains

senses.definition: Any of approximately 100 different species of fish.
senses.example: At the seafood market, the fishmonger showed us a fresh snapper caught off the coast.

senses.definition: The fish Chrysophrys auratus, especially an adult of the species.
senses.example: On our trip to New Zealand, we caught a big snapper off the coast near Auckland.

senses.definition: Any of the family Lutjanidae of percoid fishes, especially the red snapper.
senses.example: Grilled red snapper with lemon and herbs was the highlight of our anniversary dinner.

senses.definition: A small bluefish.
senses.example: The kids caught several tiny snappers, really just young bluefish, off the jetty this morning.

senses.definition: The player who snaps the ball to start the play.
senses.example: The snapper fired the ball back to the quarterback, and the offense sprang into motion.

senses.definition: Small, paper-wrapped item containing a minute quantity of explosive composition coated on small bits of sand, which explodes noisily when thrown onto a hard surface.
senses.example: The kids lit a snapper and threw it at the sidewalk, startling the whole block.

senses.definition: One who takes snaps; a photographer.
senses.example: The paparazzi were the usual snappers outside the hotel, shouting for the actor to look over.

senses.definition: The snapping turtle.
The green woodpecker, or yaffle (Picus viridis).
senses.example: Birdwatchers in England often hear the snapper before they spot it in the old oak trees.

senses.definition: A snap beetle (family Elateridae).
senses.example: Under the porch light we found a snapper beetle that flipped into the air with a click.

senses.definition: A string bean.
senses.example: Grandma filled the bowl with fresh snappers from her garden for Sunday dinner.

senses.definition: The vulva.
A punchline.
senses.example: The comedian waited for the crowd to settle before delivering the snapper that ended the joke.

senses.definition: A stumble, a trip.
senses.example: She took a snapper on the cracked sidewalk and nearly dropped her grocery bags.

senses.definition: An error, a blunder, especially a moral slip-up.
senses.example: Missing the deadline was a costly snapper that our manager never let us forget.

senses.definition: (historical) A telegraphic device with a flexible metal tongue for producing clicks like those of the sounder.
senses.example: Before the sounder took over, the operator relied on a snapper to click out messages.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: A supporter of Senator Hill's premature scheduling of the Democratic National Committee convention of 1892.
senses.example: In 1892 the party's snappers pushed Senator Hill's early convention schedule through the committee.

senses.definition: To stumble, to trip.
To fall into error; to make a mistake, and especially to stumble morally.

core.definition: A popular food fish from warm waters, especially red snapper, often served grilled or fried in restaurants.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SNAP, and make the final syllable a light 'er,' the American r-colored vowel. Don't add an extra vowel between p and e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing seafood on a menu.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use snapper for red snapper, a common fish on restaurant menus and in seafood markets, especially in the South and Gulf Coast. Many people order it by name without saying red. Snapper is also a general term for other snapper species, so a waiter may ask whether you want red or another kind.

distinctions.note: Grouper is a different large fish with a thicker, mild flesh, while snapper is a more firm, mild fish often sold as red snapper.
Tilapia is a cheaper freshwater fish; snapper is a saltwater fish with a more distinctive texture.

examples.everyday: I'll have the snapper, grilled, with the lemon butter, please.
examples.professional: The wholesaler confirmed that red snapper will be back on the order for Friday's menu.
examples.analytical: Snapper stocks in the Gulf of Mexico have been at the center of fisheries management debates.

nuance.analogy: Snapper is like a sturdy, mild white fish that holds together well on the grill, a bit like a reliable workhorse on the menu.
nuance.etymology: From snap, meaning to bite or seize quickly, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'snapper fish' as if 'snapper' were a separate word; the fish itself is snapper.
Ordering 'snapper' without specifying red, which can confuse a restaurant.

senses.definition: One who sniffs.
senses.example: The old sniffer hound followed the trail of the fox through the woods.

senses.definition: The nose.
senses.example: Wipe that dirt off your sniffer before you go to the party.

senses.definition: A software or hardware tool for intercepting and logging network traffic.
senses.example: The security team deployed a packet sniffer to log traffic on the office network.

core.definition: A program or device that intercepts and logs network traffic so the data passing through it can be inspected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is a light, r-colored schwa, not a strong 'fur' vowel, and the short i in the first syllable should not stretch into 'snee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical settings, but negative when the context is a hacker stealing passwords or private data.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday talk, a sniffer is a person or dog that sniffs, which is playful or mildly rude. In IT and security, 'packet sniffer' is the standard term, and Americans usually say it with a network admin or security team. Without a clear context, people may assume you mean a malicious tool.

distinctions.note: A sniffer passively captures traffic as it passes, while a scanner actively probes hosts to find open ports.
A sniffer captures raw traffic, while an analyzer also decodes and interprets the captured packets.

examples.everyday: Our dog is a great sniffer; he found the sandwich under the couch.
examples.professional: Let's run a packet sniffer on the staging server to see why the API calls keep timing out.
examples.analytical: The sniffer's log showed plaintext credentials, which is the strongest argument for encrypting that protocol.

nuance.analogy: A sniffer is like a security camera for data: it records everything that passes by on the wire.
nuance.etymology: From sniff, of imitative origin, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'sniffer' for a person who is sniffing in everyday speech without context; say 'he is sniffing' instead.
Assuming a packet sniffer is always illegal; it is legal on networks you own or are authorized to monitor, but not otherwise.

senses.definition: Making a snorting sound.

core.definition: Making a snorting sound, or characterized by loud, forceful snorts, especially in laughter or annoyance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, keep the r clear, and end with a light 'ee' sound. Do not turn the t into a d, because it begins the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes an audible habit and can suggest scornful or indignant behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use snorty informally to describe a laugh or a tone of voice, such as 'a snorty laugh' or 'a snorty little dog.' It is casual and descriptive, and it can imply the speaker is making fun of someone. It is not commonly used in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Snooty means snobbish; snorty means making snorting sounds. Learners often confuse them because they look alike.
Snotty means rude or contemptuous, often in a childish way; snorty describes the sound of snorting.

examples.everyday: My sister has this snorty laugh that gets everybody going at the dinner table.
examples.professional: Our lead engineer let out a snorty laugh when he saw the budget, which was not a good sign.
examples.analytical: The critic's snorty tone undermined his argument, since his scorn distracted from the evidence he claimed to examine.

nuance.analogy: A snorty laugh is like a bull blowing air through its nose: loud, quick, and impossible to miss.
nuance.etymology: From snort, with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Confusing snorty (making snorting sounds) with snooty (snobbish).
Using snorty to mean rude; the rude word is snotty.

senses.definition: A person who performs a solo.
A solo artist, one who is not in a band.
senses.example: The orchestra's soloist received a standing ovation after the difficult violin concerto.

core.definition: A musician or performer who plays or sings a featured solo part, often with an orchestra, choir or other ensemble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH. The ending is /ɪst/, with a short i, not the schwa /əst/ in the given item, so say it as 'ist' like the end of 'artist'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a respected role, often a featured performer, and suggests skill and prominence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soloist mostly for classical musicians who perform with an orchestra, and also for featured singers in choirs or musicals. For a popular singer who performs without a band, Americans more often say solo artist. A natural remark after a concert is 'She was an amazing soloist.'

distinctions.note: A soloist is usually a featured performer within an ensemble or orchestra. A solo artist is a singer or musician who performs alone without being in a band.
A lead singer fronts a band and is a permanent member. A soloist is a guest or featured performer who plays a specific solo part.

examples.everyday: My sister was the soloist in her church choir's Christmas concert, and everyone cried at the end.
examples.professional: We need to confirm the soloist's rehearsal schedule before the gala, since she only has two free weeks.
examples.analytical: The concerto places the soloist in dialogue with the orchestra, so the work's meaning depends on how the performer negotiates that relationship.

nuance.analogy: A soloist is like the one voice that rises above a choir at the climax of a song.
nuance.etymology: From solo with the suffix -ist, meaning one who performs.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as schwa, /əst/, instead of /ɪst/.
Using soloist for a band member who simply plays a lot, when it refers to a featured solo role.

senses.definition: Somehow.

core.definition: In some way or manner; somehow, even if the method is not known or specified.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUM, and keep the second syllable as a clear way with a light secondary stress. Do not reduce it to 'sum-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to casual. It sounds relaxed and vague, which is fine in conversation but less polished in writing.
nuance.usage_note: Someway is chiefly spoken and informal, and you will hear it most often in everyday talk, sometimes in the phrase 'someway or another'. In careful writing, Americans usually choose somehow instead. Using someway in a meeting or a formal email may sound casual, so save it for conversation.

distinctions.note: Somehow is the standard form in both speech and writing; someway is informal and less common, and it means essentially the same thing.
Anyway means regardless or in any case, or it changes the subject; someway means by some method, which is a different meaning.

examples.everyday: We'll get the couch up the stairs someway, even if it takes all afternoon.
examples.professional: I don't have the exact number yet, but we'll get the data cleaned someway before Friday.
examples.analytical: The argument does not explain how knowledge arises, only that someway the mind must reach beyond its own ideas.

nuance.analogy: Like a path through the woods that you have not mapped but know must lead somewhere.
nuance.etymology: Formed from some and way, with the same sense as somehow.
common_mistakes: Using someway in formal writing, where somehow is expected.
Writing it as two words ('some way') when you mean the adverb 'somehow'; as an adverb, the one-word form is more usual in casual speech.

senses.definition: A state of drowsiness or sleepiness.

core.definition: A state of drowsiness or sleepiness, often a heavy or lingering one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllables are reduced to a weak uh. Do not pronounce the final -ence as 'ens' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, because it suggests a heavy or unwanted state of sleepiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use somnolence mainly in medical, scientific, or literary writing, such as a drug warning or a novel. In everyday talk they say drowsiness or just sleepy. The word can sound stiff in casual conversation, but it fits well in a report about medication side effects.

distinctions.note: Drowsiness is the everyday word for feeling sleepy; somnolence is more formal and often describes a deeper or more lasting state.
Sleepiness is a plain, neutral term; somnolence is more clinical and is often used about side effects or medical conditions.

examples.everyday: After that heavy lunch I felt a wave of somnolence and could barely keep my eyes open.
examples.professional: Daytime somnolence is a common side effect, so the warning label needs to be clear.
examples.analytical: Ancient writers treated somnolence as the threshold between wakefulness and the mysteries of dreaming.

nuance.analogy: Like a fog that rolls over the mind and slowly dims its light.
nuance.etymology: From Latin somnolentia, from somnolentus 'sleepy', from somnus 'sleep'.
common_mistakes: Using somnolence for everyday tiredness in casual speech, where drowsiness or sleepy is more natural.
Confusing the noun somnolence with the adjective somnolent when a noun is needed.

somnolence.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *somnolence*, from Late Latin *somnolentia*, derived from Latin *somnus* (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European **swépnos* (“sleep, slumber”).

senses.definition: Any musical composition.
Poetical composition; poetry; verse.
senses.example: She memorized the long song of Homer for her classics exam.

senses.definition: The act or art of singing.
senses.example: The evening was filled with laughter, dancing, and joyful song around the campfire.

senses.definition: A melodious sound made by a bird, insect, whale or other animal.
senses.example: I love hearing the song of canary birds.

senses.definition: A low price, especially one under the expected value; chiefly in for a song.
senses.example: He bought that car for a song.

senses.definition: A musical composition with lyrics for voice or voices, performed by singing.
senses.example: Thomas listened to his favorite song on the radio yesterday.

senses.definition: The distinctive sound that a male bird utters to attract a mate or to protect his territory; contrasts with call; also, similar vocalisations made by female birds.
senses.example: Early each spring, the male cardinal sings his bright song from the top of the oak.

core.definition: A short piece of music with words, meant to be sung. Also, any piece of music for the voice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the vowel open, like 'saw' rather than 'sew'. Make the ng one sound at the end, and do not add a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Positive and neutral; it is a warm, everyday word for music and poetry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use song for everything from pop tunes to folk music and hymns, and it appears in everyday talk about the radio, concerts, and playlists. The idiom 'for a song' means very cheaply, and 'on song' means performing well, which is more common in British English, so Americans usually say 'in good form' or 'doing great' instead.

distinctions.note: A tune is just the melody, while a song includes words meant to be sung.
A hymn is a song of praise, usually sung in worship, while song is a general word.

examples.everyday: Have you heard that new song on the radio? It's stuck in my head all day.
examples.professional: Our marketing team wrote a short song for the campaign, and it tested well with the focus groups.
examples.analytical: A hymn is a song addressed to God, so its theology matters as much as its melody.

nuance.analogy: A song is a short story carried by a melody, so the tune helps the words stay in memory.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sang, related to 'sing'.
common_mistakes: Using 'many song' instead of 'many songs', because song is countable.
Confusing the vowel with 'sing', which has a short i sound, rather than song's open vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the usual word is shir, meaning a song or poem sung. Exodus 15 describes Moses and the Israelites singing after crossing the sea, and the Psalms include many songs of praise and lament. Psalm 40 speaks of God giving the singer a new song, meaning a fresh cause for thanksgiving. The Song of Solomon, a love poem in the Hebrew Bible, takes its title from the word song in its superlative sense, the finest of songs.

song.etymology: From Middle English *song*, *sang*, from Old English *sang*, from **sangu*, from Proto-Germanic **sangwaz* (“singing, song”), from Proto-Indo-European **sengʷʰ-* (“to sing”).

senses.definition: Any inflammation of the pharynx that causes soreness.
senses.example: I woke up with a sore throat that made swallowing coffee painful.

senses.definition: The same, as a common symptom for many viral and bacterial infections.
senses.example: Doctors say a sore throat is one of the most common early symptoms of the flu.

core.definition: Pain, scratchiness, or soreness in the throat, usually a symptom of a cold, flu, or infection.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun the main stress falls on sore, not throat, so say SAWR THROHT with the stronger beat on the first word. Throat rhymes with boat, not with the vowel in cot.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common, everyday medical complaint and is not alarming unless it is severe or lasts a long time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I have a sore throat in everyday conversation, at work, or on the phone when calling in sick. Doctors may ask whether you have a sore throat along with a fever or cough. The phrase is neutral and polite; a natural reply is Feel better soon or I hope you feel better.

distinctions.note: Strep throat is a specific bacterial infection caused by Streptococcus, while sore throat is a general symptom that many illnesses can cause.
Laryngitis is inflammation of the larynx that mainly affects the voice, while a sore throat is pain in the throat itself.

collocations: a sore throat and a cough

examples.everyday: I can't come to the party tonight because I have a sore throat and a fever.
examples.professional: I'm going to work from home today since I have a sore throat, so please send me the notes.
examples.analytical: A sore throat is a nonspecific symptom, so clinicians rely on other signs to decide whether a viral or bacterial cause is likely.

nuance.analogy: A sore throat is like a smoke alarm: it signals that something is inflamed nearby, but it does not tell you exactly what caused the fire.
nuance.etymology: Sore comes from Old English sar, 'painful'; throat comes from Old English throte.
common_mistakes: Saying sore throat with stress on throat, which sounds unnatural to American ears.
Using sore for sour or saying I have sore throat without the article a.

conversation.text: I have a sore throat, so I'm going to drink some hot tea.
My sore throat started yesterday after the game.
Salt water helps a sore throat feel better.

senses.definition: The action of the verb to sound.
senses.example: The sounding of the ship's horn echoed across the harbor at dusk.

senses.definition: A test made with a probe or sonde.
senses.example: The geologist's soil sounding revealed a dense clay layer about two meters down.

senses.definition: A measured depth of water.
senses.example: The sailor took a sounding every five minutes

senses.definition: Any place or part of the ocean, or other water, where a sounding line will reach the bottom.
senses.example: The captain's chart showed a deep sounding of two hundred fathoms just past the reef.

senses.definition: The sand, shells, etc. brought up by the sounding lead when it has touched bottom.
senses.example: The sounding came up with grey sand and broken shells stuck to the lead.

senses.definition: The act of inserting of a thin metal rod into the urethra of the penis for medical or sexual purposes.
senses.example: The urologist performed a sounding to check for a blockage in the urethra before the procedure.

senses.definition: Emitting a sound.
senses.example: The sounding bell woke me up.

senses.definition: Sonorous.
senses.example: The cathedral's sounding bells filled the square with a deep, resonant tone.

core.definition: A measurement of water depth taken by dropping a weighted line or probe to find how deep the water is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'ow' is a diphthong that starts open and glides toward 'oo', and the final -ing is a short, light vowel rather than 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from navigation or Scripture.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English this sense is mostly found in maritime, historical, or biblical contexts. In everyday speech Americans would say depth reading or water depth. The word also appears as a verb form, as in 'sounding the alarm,' but that sense is different.

distinctions.note: Sound as a verb means to measure depth or to make a noise; sounding as a noun names the measurement itself in navigation.
Soundings is the plural form and is more common when referring to a set of depth measurements on a chart.

examples.everyday: The fisherman said he took a quick sounding before dropping anchor near the rocks.
examples.professional: The survey crew recorded sounding data at each buoy to update the harbor chart.
examples.analytical: The narrator's reference to a sounding line becomes a metaphor for testing the depth of a character's faith.

nuance.analogy: Like tapping a wall to find out how thick it is: you measure something unseen by sending a probe down into it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb sound, from Old English sundian, meaning to measure the depth of water.
common_mistakes: Using sounding to mean the sound a thing makes; that meaning is the noun sound.
Confusing it with soundness, which means logical validity or health.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb bolizō, 'to take soundings' or 'heave the lead,' appears in the account of Paul's shipwreck. Acts 27:27-28 describes sailors sounding the depth of the water as they approach land. Job 38:16 asks whether God has entered the springs of the sea, pointing to the unseen depths that only God fully knows.

senses.definition: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flat surface attached to a long handle, used for turning, lifting, or stirring food.
senses.example: Scrape the batter off the sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula.

senses.definition: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flexible surface attached to a long handle, used for scraping the sides of bowls.
senses.example: Scrape the batter off the sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula.

senses.definition: A croupier's tool for turning up cards in a casino.
senses.example: The dealer used a spatula to slide the cards face up across the blackjack table.

senses.definition: A thin hand tool, often made of nickel, for handling chemicals or other materials, when weighing, etc.
senses.example: The chemist weighed the powder on a balance, then transferred it with a metal spatula.

senses.definition: A sclerotized, T-shaped plate in the prothorax of larvae of flies belonging to family Cecidomyiidae, the gall midges.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the larva's sclerotized spatula was clearly visible in the prothorax.

senses.definition: (dated) A palette knife.
senses.example: The old painter cleaned his brushes and scraped the wet oils off his spatula.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To lift with or as if with a spatula.
senses.example: Carefully spatula the fish fillet onto the plate so it stays intact.

senses.definition: To strike with a spatula.
senses.example: The angry chef spatulaed the boy's hand when he reached into the pan.

core.definition: A kitchen tool with a flat, wide blade on a long handle, used for flipping, lifting, or spreading food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle sound is ch, as in chair, not the y sound of British speech, so say SPACH-uh-luh rather than spat-yoo-luh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spatula constantly for kitchen tasks such as flipping pancakes or scraping a pan. A metal one is often called a turner in some regions, and a rubber one is called a spatula too, so you can say a rubber spatula to be clear. The word is ordinary and not formal.

distinctions.note: Turner is a term used in some regions for a flat spatula for flipping food, while spatula is the standard term across the US.
A scraper is often a flat tool for removing material from a surface, while a spatula is mainly used for cooking or baking.

examples.everyday: Can you hand me the spatula so I can flip these pancakes?
examples.professional: The kitchen staff keep a spare spatula at each station to avoid cross-contamination.
examples.analytical: The chef's spatula is a small instrument, but its design shapes how the dish is plated.

nuance.analogy: Like a flat paddle that scoops and turns food the way a shovel moves sand.
nuance.etymology: From Latin spatula, a diminutive of spatha, 'broad blade.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a y sound (spat-yoo-luh), which is British-leaning and less natural in US speech.
Confusing spatula with spoon when you need a flat tool for flipping.

spatula.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *spatula* (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of *spatha* (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek *σπάθη* (“a broad wood or metal blade”). compare *spatha* and *spathe*.

senses.definition: Of a horse: having spavin (“a disease of horses caused by a bony swelling which develops in a leg due to inflammation”).
senses.example: The farmer walked the spavined mare slowly to the barn, favoring her swollen hind leg.

senses.definition: Of a person: lame due to a leg disease.
Of a person or a thing: old, worn-out; also, obsolete.
senses.example: I’m a spavined old warrior, and I don’t have much time left in this world, but I still have a few tricks to teach these whippersnappers.

core.definition: Describing an old, worn-out, or broken-down horse, or a person or thing that is lame or decrepit. The term is rare and mostly literary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The vowel is short, as in 'hat', and the final 'ed' is pronounced as a single syllable 'ind', not 'ed'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests decrepitude, decay, or shabbiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday speech. You will meet it in older fiction, in descriptions of rural life, or in writing that wants a vivid, old-fashioned image. For a plain modern equivalent, say 'worn-out', 'broken-down', or 'decrepit'.

distinctions.note: Decrepit is common and general, describing anything worn down by age or neglect. Spavined is rare and literary, and it is most often used of horses or old machines.
Lame is a broad, everyday word for a limp or impaired leg. Spavined adds the sense of an old, worn-out body or thing.

examples.professional: The auditor called the legacy billing system spavined and ready for replacement.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses the spavined horse as an emblem of a dying rural economy.

nuance.analogy: A spavined horse is like a car with a bad engine and rusted frame, still running but clearly past its prime.
nuance.etymology: From spavin, a disease of horses' legs, from Old French espavain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'spah-VINED' with stress on the second syllable.
Using it for ordinary tiredness; it describes age or decay, not simple fatigue.

spavined.etymology: From Late Middle English *spaueyned*, from *spavein*, *spaveine* (“swelling on horse’s leg causing lameness; disease causing lameness in horses”) + *-ed*.

senses.definition: One who speaks.
senses.example: There were three different speakers, but I couldn't make out their accents.

senses.definition: Loudspeaker.
senses.example: She lost her hearing after standing too close to the speaker at the festival.

senses.definition: Speakerphone.
senses.example: you're on speaker

senses.definition: The chair or presiding officer of certain legislative bodies, such as the U.K. House of Commons or the U.S. House of Representatives.
senses.example: The Speaker of the House gaveled the chamber to order at noon before the budget debate began.

senses.definition: One who makes a speech to an audience.
senses.example: hired speaker; motivational speaker

senses.definition: A book containing passages of text for use in speeches.
senses.example: Before writing his sermon, the pastor pulled a speaker of famous inaugural addresses from the shelf.

senses.definition: The producer of a given utterance, whether speech or text.
senses.example: Popular culture often incorrectly attributes quotes from the speakers of poems or songs to the authors thereof, as when "I took the one less traveled by" is attributed to Robert Frost rather than to the speaker in Frost's "The Road Not Taken".

senses.definition: The literary character uttering the lyrics of a poem or song, as opposed to the author writing the words of that character.
senses.example: Popular culture often incorrectly attributes quotes from the speakers of poems or songs to the authors thereof, as when "I took the one less traveled by" is attributed to Robert Frost rather than to the speaker in Frost's "The Road Not Taken".

senses.definition: A key on a woodwind instrument of the clarinet family (compare octave key on other instruments) which induces the instrument to overblow.
senses.example: When the clarinet's upper register sounds thin, the player should check that the speaker key opens fully.

core.definition: A person who talks or gives a talk to an audience, or a device that produces sound.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SPEEK. The final -er is a light, rhotic syllable, so avoid saying 'speak-ah' with a clear a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a person or device without any judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use speaker for a presenter at a conference, a person who gives a talk, or a device such as a Bluetooth speaker or a smart speaker. In a meeting, you might say Our guest speaker is joining us at ten. For a loudspeaker or speakerphone, Americans often say the speaker or put it on speaker. Native English speakers may also use the word for someone who talks in a particular language.

distinctions.note: An orator is a skilled public speaker, often formal and rhetorical, while speaker is a neutral, everyday word.
A presenter usually shows slides or demonstrates something in a workplace setting, while a speaker may give a general talk to an audience.

examples.everyday: The speaker on my laptop is so quiet, can you turn it up for me?
examples.professional: Our keynote speaker is confirmed for Thursday, so please send her the slides by Monday.
examples.analytical: The speaker's authority in this essay rests less on evidence than on his claimed personal experience.

nuance.analogy: A speaker is like a megaphone for a voice: the person or device carries the message to the people who need to hear it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sprecan, to speak, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying native speaker of English when the context is clearly language; native English speaker is the more precise term.
Confusing speaker with speech, which is the noun for the talk itself.

speaker.etymology: From Middle English *speker*, *spekere*, an alteration of Old English *speca*, *spreca* (“speaker”), from Proto-Germanic **sprekô* (“speaker”), equivalent to *speak* + *-er*.

senses.definition: A tiny spot or particle, especially of dirt.
senses.example: a tiny speck of soot

senses.definition: A very small amount; a particle; a whit.
senses.example: He has not a speck of money.

senses.definition: A small etheostomoid fish, Etheostoma stigmaeum, common in the eastern United States.
senses.example: Anglers in the Ozarks often find the speck hiding beneath rocks in shallow creeks.

senses.definition: Fat; lard; fat meat.
senses.example: Grandma kept a jar of speck by the stove for frying cornbread and greens.

senses.definition: A juniper-flavored ham originally from Tyrol.
senses.example: At the deli counter, she ordered thin slices of speck for the charcuterie board.

senses.definition: The blubber of whales or other marine mammals.
senses.example: Whalers rendered the speck from the whale into oil for lamps and soap.

senses.definition: The fat of the hippopotamus.
senses.example: The old trader's journal described rubbing hippopotamus speck onto leather boots to keep them supple.

senses.definition: To mark with specks; to speckle.
senses.example: paper specked by impurities in the water used in its manufacture

core.definition: A very small spot or particle, especially of dirt, dust, or stain.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like 'e' in 'bed', and the final 'k' is clearly released. Do not stretch the vowel into 'speck' with a long sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes something tiny, often in a physical sense, though it can be used to suggest a very small amount.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'speck' in everyday talk about dust, dirt, or a tiny mark on a surface, such as 'a speck of dust on my glasses.' It is also used figuratively for a very small amount, usually in phrases like 'not a speck of.' It is a common, plain word, and no formal tone is needed.

distinctions.note: A spot is a broader word for a mark or blemish on a surface, while a speck is smaller and often refers to a tiny particle.
A fleck is a small patch or particle of color or material, often on something else, while a speck is usually a tiny dot of dirt or dust.

examples.everyday: There's a speck of dust on your glasses, so let me wipe it off for you.
examples.professional: The inspector flagged a speck of debris on the circuit board before we shipped the batch.
examples.analytical: Augustine's image of a speck in another's eye and a beam in one's own turns the reader's attention back on the self.

nuance.analogy: A speck is like a single grain of sand on a white beach, noticeable only when you look closely.
nuance.etymology: Middle English speck, probably from Old English specca, 'spot, stain.'
common_mistakes: Using 'speck' for a large spot, where 'spot' or 'stain' is more natural.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long 'ee' sound, which changes the word.
nuance.biblical_note: In Matthew 7:3-5 and Luke 6:41-42 Jesus speaks of a speck in a brother's eye and a log in one's own eye. The Greek word is karphos, meaning a dry stalk, straw, or chip of wood, and the passage warns against judging others while ignoring one's own faults. The RSV uses 'speck' to render this small piece of debris.

speck.etymology: From Middle English *spekke*, from Old English *specca* (“small spot, stain”), from the same ultimate source as Proto-Germanic **sprakô* (“spark”).

senses.definition: Dapper; fine or neat, especially in style of clothing or other appearance.
senses.example: Dan showed up to the wedding in a spiffy navy suit and matching pocket square.

senses.definition: A dapper person.
senses.example: The old barber greeted every customer like a spiffy who had stepped out of a magazine.

core.definition: Neat, stylish and smart in appearance, usually in a cheerful, old-fashioned way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a short 'i' sound, like 'sit'. The final syllable is a light 'ee', and the word is only two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises someone's neat, sharp look. It can sound playful or a little old-fashioned, so it is not used for serious or formal things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spiffy in casual conversation about clothes, cars or a freshly cleaned room, often with a friendly tone. A common phrase is 'You look spiffy!' and a natural reply is 'Thanks, I just got it cleaned.' Younger speakers may find it dated, so it sounds warm and retro rather than modern.

distinctions.note: Sharp is the more common American word for well-dressed or neat, while spiffy sounds more playful and old-fashioned.
Dapper suggests a neat, stylish man in a refined way, while spiffy can describe clothes, cars or objects too.

examples.everyday: You look spiffy in that blue shirt, so where are you going tonight?
examples.professional: The team's new slide deck looks spiffy, but the numbers in it are what the executives will judge.
examples.analytical: A spiffy presentation can impress an audience, but it cannot replace careful evidence.

nuance.analogy: Spiffy is like a freshly polished shoe: neat, bright and ready for a good occasion.
common_mistakes: Using spiffy for serious or formal situations, where it sounds too casual.
Confusing spiffy with spicy, which is about hot or flavorful food.

senses.definition: A curve that is the locus of a point that rotates about a fixed point while continuously increasing its distance from that point.
senses.example: On graph paper, the spiral starts at the origin and widens with each turn.

senses.definition: A helix.
senses.example: The staircase wound up the tower in a tight spiral of cast iron.

senses.definition: A self-sustaining process with a lot of momentum involved, so it is difficult to accelerate or stop it at once.
senses.example: Once rumors of layoffs started, the company's morale entered a downward spiral.

senses.definition: A section of track that forms a circle and crosses over itself, used for gaining height in mountainous territory.
senses.example: The mountain railway built a spiral so trains could climb the steep grade.

senses.definition: Helical, like a spiral.
senses.example: The spiral staircase in the lighthouse was too narrow for the movers' dresser.

senses.definition: To move along the path of a spiral or helix.
senses.example: The falling leaves spiraled down from the tree.

senses.definition: To cause something to spiral.
senses.example: You need to learn how to spiral a ball.

senses.definition: To increase continually.
senses.example: Her debts were spiralling out of control.

senses.definition: To decline mentally.
senses.example: She spiraled into a deep depression.

core.definition: A curve that winds around a central point while moving farther from it, like a coil, a snail shell or a staircase.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SPY. The r is clear and rhotic, and the final -al is a reduced syllable that sounds like 'uhl', not 'ahl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a shape. In phrases like downward spiral, it carries a clearly negative tone about a worsening situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spiral for spiral staircases, spiral notebooks and the shape of shells. The phrase downward spiral is common in news and in conversations about worsening problems, such as debt or depression. People also say spiral out of control, with spiral as a verb.

distinctions.note: A helix is the precise term for a three-dimensional spiral, like a DNA strand or a screw thread; spiral is broader and often used for flat curves.
Coil usually means a loop of material, like wire or a spring; spiral describes the shape of the path.
A vortex is a whirling mass of water or air; spiral is a shape that can describe a vortex's path.

examples.everyday: The staircase in the old house is a narrow spiral, so be careful when you go up in the dark.
examples.professional: The data plot shows a spiral pattern, so each sample drifts slightly farther from the center as the trial goes on.
examples.analytical: Dante's ascent of Mount Purgatory is pictured as a spiral, moving upward while circling the same mountain terraces.

nuance.analogy: Think of a snail shell: the curl winds outward from the tip, getting wider with each turn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin spiralis, from spira, coil, from Greek speira.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'spy-RAL'.
Writing spiraled with two l's; the American spelling uses one l.

spiral.etymology: From Middle French *spirale*, from Medieval Latin *spiralis*, from Latin *spīra*, from Ancient Greek *σπεῖρα* (“wreath, coil, twist”).

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see spoiler,‎ alert: a warning that plot elements in a drama will be exposed.
senses.example: Spoiler alert: the detective is the killer, so stop reading if you want to be surprised.

senses.definition: An indication, placed in a text, that the plot of a drama is about to be exposed.
senses.example: Spoiler alert: The main character, Mark, succumbs to an illness at the end.

senses.definition: Indicates that the speaker is about to reveal something unanticipated or unpleasant.
senses.example: Spoiler alert, these measures have not proved to be very helpful at mitigating the effects of this crisis.

core.definition: A warning that you are about to reveal information, usually the ending of a movie, show or book, before someone hears it.

pronunciation.tip: Two stress groups: 'SPOY' is strongest in the first word and 'LERT' in the second. Link the words smoothly and reduce the 'uh' in 'alert' so it sounds like 'uh-LERT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or friendly. It is a courtesy warning that signals care for others' enjoyment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Spoiler alert!' before revealing something about a show, movie, game or book, often online or in conversation. It is casual and playful, so it is not appropriate in formal writing. A natural reply is 'Thanks for the warning' or simply 'Okay, I'll stop.' It can also be used humorously before unpleasant news.

distinctions.note: 'Warning' is general and can be serious, while 'spoiler alert' is light and specific to plot reveals.

examples.everyday: Spoiler alert: the dog doesn't make it in the end.
examples.professional: Spoiler alert: the client already saw the revised numbers, so we should discuss them now.
examples.analytical: A spoiler alert signals that the text will expose a structure that the reader might otherwise prefer to discover.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign that says 'wet paint' before you touch the wall, it protects people from an unwanted surprise.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'spoiler' and 'alert', from the Latin root 'alerta' meaning on the lookout.
common_mistakes: Saying 'spoiler alert' in a formal presentation where it sounds too casual.
Pronouncing 'alert' with full stress, instead of the stressed second syllable 'LERT' with a reduced first syllable.

conversation.text: Spoiler alert: the main character dies at the end.
Spoiler alert, they get back together in the last episode.
Spoiler alert: I didn't actually go to the gym today.

senses.definition: To get ready for a fight.
To adopt a fighting stance.
To face (someone) in a contest.
To pay back money that is owed.
senses.example: Let me know how much my share in the activity is and I'll square up with you tomorrow.

senses.definition: To mill (blocks, inserts, etc) into precisely square condition.
senses.example: The machinist squared up the aluminum blocks on the mill before drilling.

core.definition: To take a fighting stance, or to face someone directly in a confrontation or contest.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on up, which is a strong, clear syllable. Square is lightly stressed and linked into up, so it sounds like 'skwair-UP'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or aggressive when describing a physical or verbal confrontation. Neutral or even businesslike when used for settling accounts.
